oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches bochurim that Torah is the mind and tefillah the heart of a Jew's spiritual life, and that in the generation before Moshiach heartfelt, even loud, davening is what revives a person and makes his learning pure.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the two organs that give life to the body, the mind and the heart, and compares them to Torah and tefillah. From the Gemara's teaching that tefillah is the 'service of the heart' he shows that davening with the lips alone is not davening. Real tefillah needs effort and concentration, and it is the path to dveikus, which he defines as speaking with Hashem; for our generation it means pouring out one's heart. He describes the sweetness of such davening, citing Tehillim and Yedid Nefesh. Then he explains why, in the time before Moshiach, tefillah is needed even more than Torah, with the parable of a sick man who needs orange juice rather than bread and meat. A story of a young man who learned ten years 'for the cats' warns against learning to show off; learning for Hashem depends on davening well. He ends with loud davening, a Chortkov story, and a brachah to the bochurim.

en: Torah corresponds to the mind and tefillah to the heart; a Jew's spiritual life needs both, just as a body cannot live without either organ.
Tefillah is the 'service of the heart', so saying the words with the lips alone, even with their meaning in mind, is not yet davening.
Heartfelt davening brings a person to dveikus, cleaving to Hashem, which the Rav describes as speaking with Him; for our generation it means pouring out one's heart to Him.
In the time before Moshiach tefillah is needed even more than Torah, and even bochurim, who must toil in Gemara, need it as part of Klal Yisroel.
Learning must be refined, for Hashem's sake and not to show off, and one cannot learn this way without davening well first.

title.en: Mind and heart: Torah and tefillah

summary.en: The Rav compares Torah and tefillah to the mind and heart that give life to the body. From the Gemara's teaching that tefillah is the service of the heart, he shows that davening with the mouth alone, even with the meaning in mind, is not real davening.

title.en: Davening with effort, not in a rush

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shulchan Aruch on davening with detachment from the physical, a level not everyone reaches, and explains that davening with the heart cannot be done in a rush. Great tzaddikim can daven quickly, but ordinary people must invest effort and concentrate.

title.en: Dveikus: speaking with Hashem

summary.en: The Rav defines dveikus as speaking with Hashem, a yichud, and says all the mitzvos are counsels to reach it. Great tzaddikim were lost in Hashem; in our low generation dveikus means pouring out one's heart, feeling that Hashem loves and listens, and this is the service of the heart.

title.en: The sweetness of real tefillah

summary.en: The Rav says even simple people can merit moments of tefillah sweeter than any pleasure, citing Tehillim and Yedid Nefesh. Saying Yedid Nefesh in a rush means little, but after preparing for Shabbos properly it can be said with truth; he mentions bochurim who shed tears of love while davening.

title.en: Tefillah in the generation before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that although Torah is the highest yichud, tefillah's dveikus is stronger, and before Moshiach tefillah is more important. With the parable of a sick man who needs orange juice, he shows that Klal Yisroel in its 'old age' needs tefillah, and so do bochurim who must toil in Gemara.

title.en: Ten years of learning for the cats

summary.en: The Rav says Torah must be refined, learned for Hashem, not to show off with questions and answers. He tells a story from Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz about a young man who learned day and night for ten years thinking his father-in-law was listening overhead, and found only a family of cats in the attic.

title.en: Learning lishmah needs davening

summary.en: The Rav says one must at least know that one learns for Hashem, and that refined learning comes only after davening well; then the Gemara is felt as holy. He brings the Beis Aharon that tefillah and learning each need the other, like mind and heart, and contrasts Moshe Rabbeinu, head of the learners, with Dovid HaMelech, head of those who daven.

title.en: Loud davening, and a closing brachah

summary.en: The Rav explains that quiet or loud davening follows each Rebbe's root of the soul, telling of a Karliner chassid in Chortkov whose heartfelt shouting the Rebbe praised. He says that today davening is like Ne'ilah and one must daven loud to warm oneself, and ends with a brachah to bochurim going to Eretz Yisroel.

oneLiner.en: The Rav applies the Gemara's rule that one who takes a path of temptation when another path exists is called a rasha to the use of smartphones, and teaches that the whole Torah turns on obeying the Sages of each generation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk in Yeshaya praising one who shuts his eyes from seeing evil, and the Gemara that applies it to a man who passes women washing clothes at the river. If he had another road and chose this one, Rashbam says he is a rasha even if he closes his eyes; only when there is no other way may he go. The Rav applies this to a smartphone: if business truly requires it, he may use it with great care, but if a plain phone with a hechsher would do, he earns that title. He then turns to the obligation to obey the Sages of every generation: the Rambam and the passuk 'al pi haTorah', the Gemara in Eruvin, and the Gemara in Berachos on eating before Maariv. Shaarei Teshuvah explains that disobeying the Sages comes from belittling them. This, he says, is the axis of the Torah, the middle passuk of Devarim. The story of Shlomo HaMelech shows the danger of relying on oneself; one who submits to the Sages gains Hashem's help against the yetzer hara.

en: One who walks a road of temptation when he could have taken another road is called a rasha, even if he shuts his eyes and does not look.
The Rav applies this to a smartphone: one who truly needs it for business may use it with care, but one who could manage with a plain phone with a hechsher falls under that title.
There is a mitzvah to obey the Sages of every generation, not only the Great Sanhedrin, including the fences and enactments they make for their time.
According to Shaarei Teshuvah, one who disobeys the Sages does so out of belittling them, and that is why Chazal treat it so severely.
Submitting to the Sages of the generation is the axis around which the whole Torah turns.
One who follows the Sages is helped by Hashem against the yetzer hara, while one who belittles them loses that help.

title.en: Shutting the eyes, and the smartphone

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk in Yeshaya and the Gemara about a man passing women washing clothes at the river: if he had another road, Rashbam calls him a rasha even if he does not look. He applies this to a smartphone: one who truly needs it for business may use it with care, but if a plain phone with a hechsher would do, he earns that title.

title.en: The mitzvah to obey the Sages of each generation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam on the passuk 'al pi haTorah', that one must obey not only the Great Sanhedrin but the Sages of every generation, including their fences and enactments. He adds the Gemara in Eruvin on 'chadashim gam yeshanim' and the Gemara in Berachos on eating before Maariv, and asks why that carries such a severe liability.

title.en: Shaarei Teshuvah: disobedience as contempt

summary.en: The Rav brings Shaarei Teshuvah, that one who disobeys the Sages does so because he belittles them and thinks he knows better, like the rebellious elder. He concludes that submitting to the Sages is the axis of the whole Torah, and notes that the middle passuk of Sefer Devarim is 'al pi haTorah'.

title.en: Shlomo HaMelech and help against the yetzer hara

summary.en: The Rav tells how Shlomo HaMelech relied on himself regarding the limit on a king's wives, and the yud of 'yarbeh' complained before the Kisei HaKavod. He explains that one who keeps the Torah as the Sages direct is guarded by Heaven against the yetzer hara, while one who belittles them loses that help, and closes with the blessing of long days for those who follow the Sages.

oneLiner.en: On the opening of Tanya chapter three, the Rav explains that the ten utterances of creation are the ten sefiros through which Hashem reveals Himself, and that a person carries them as intellect (Chabad) and seven character traits (Chagas Nehim).

abstract.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter three: each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah contains ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros. He starts from the Mishnah's ten utterances of creation and the Gemara's question that only nine are found, and explains that these ten are ten powers, the sefiros, through which the infinite Hashem appears to us, filtered down through the worlds like sunlight through darkened films. Man, created in the image of G-d, contains all ten, though in him they are not called sefiros but Chabad (intellect) and seven midos. He defines chesed as giving and extending, gevurah as fear and withdrawal, tiferes as a new harmony, netzach and hod as two ways of survival, yesod as the power to create. He links the seven midos to music, the seven days of creation and Shabbos, contrasts Chabad's path of intellect with other Chassidim's path of emotion, and shows that the seven midos can serve good or evil, unlike the higher three.

en: The ten utterances of creation are ten powers, the sefiros, through which the infinite Hashem reveals Himself in creation in different aspects.
Man, created in the image of G-d, contains all ten, but in him they are not called sefiros; they are divided into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim.
Chesed is extending oneself and giving; gevurah is fear and drawing into oneself; tiferes is the harmony that arises when the two meet.
Netzach and hod are two ways of survival, fighting the adversary or bending under pressure; yesod is the power to create.
Chabad, the intellect, is the father and root of the midos and is above this world, so in essence it has no evil, while the seven midos can be used for good or for evil.
Chesed and gevurah run through all of creation: male and female, summer and winter, the poles of a magnet, day and night.

title.en: Tanya chapter three and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Tanya chapter three and recalls that nefesh, ruach and neshamah each consist of ten powers. He brings the Mishnah's ten utterances of creation, the Gemara's question that only nine are found and its answers, and explains that these ten are the sefiros through which the infinite Hashem appears in creation.

title.en: From the sefiros above to man below

summary.en: With the mashal of looking at the sun through darkened films, the Rav describes how the light comes down from Atzilus to Asiyah. Man, in the image of G-d, contains the ten, but in him they are not called sefiros; the Rav shows that Adam equals the filled-out Name of Havayah and divides the ten into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah: giving and withdrawing

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chabad belongs only to man while midos are found even in animals. Chesed is love that extends itself and gives; gevurah is fear, a contraction into oneself. He applies this to the male as giver and the female as receiver, as seen in kiddushin and the kesubah.

title.en: Tiferes: a new harmony, not a mixture

summary.en: The Rav explains tiferes as the blending of chesed and gevurah, tied to the joining of mercy at the start of Bereishis and to the last utterance about a helpmate. With lemonade, a painting, a niggun and a second voice harmonizing, he shows that tiferes is a qualitatively new creation, and applies it to man and woman together.

title.en: Netzach, hod, yesod and the body

summary.en: The Rav defines netzach as surviving by fighting and hod as surviving by yielding. He brings Pasach Eliyahu from the Tikkunei Zohar, which maps the sefiros onto the body: chesed the right arm, gevurah the left, tiferes the body, netzach and hod the two legs, yesod the organ of creation and malchus the mouth, and postpones explaining malchus.

title.en: Music, the days of creation and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav compares the seven sefiros to the seven notes of music, brings the harp of seven, eight and ten strings, and the Zohar's heichal opened only by song. Each day of creation was made with one sefira; when Shabbos completes the harp, one can sing zemiros, and the seven voices of the psalm said to welcome Shabbos correspond to the sefiros.

title.en: Chabad: the mochin and the Chabad derech

summary.en: The Rav explains that chochmah, binah and da'as are mochin, the father, mother and root of the midos. He explains the name Chabad Chassidus: serving Hashem through understanding creation, while most other Chassidim worked on love, fear and praise of Hashem and were wary of delving into what is above this world.

title.en: Animals have one trait, man has all

summary.en: Everything in creation comes from one or a combination of the ten. Each animal shows one sefira, like the lion, whose name equals gevurah, or the timid sheep, while man, to whom every part of creation contributed according to the Ramban, can be anything, with one or two sefiros dominant.

title.en: The seven midos for good and for evil

summary.en: The Rav explains that the upper three are above this world and have no evil, while the seven lower midos, where the Tree of Knowledge took hold, can be good or bad. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on the passuk calling a forbidden union chesed, a judge who fears the powerful, and poetry that inflames the yetzer, and adds that the ten sons of Haman are the ten sefiros of impurity.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah in all creation; the Tanya's words

summary.en: The Rav shows chesed and gevurah throughout creation: male and female, summer and winter, positive and negative charge, the poles of a magnet pointing north and south, day and night. He then reads the Tanya's words that each level contains ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros, divided into three mothers and seven doubles, and closes with intellect and midos in the human soul.

oneLiner.en: In a talk on technology given by another speaker (R' Tauber, per the catalog title), not by the Rav, the speaker argues that a Jew who must use a device for parnassah is a soldier Hashem sent to a hard front, and may use only what he is commanded, as he is commanded.

abstract.en: This recording is a talk by another speaker (named R' Tauber in the catalog title), not by the Rav. He opens with the privilege of living in a generation led by gedolim, and says the yetzer hara changed tactics: once outside persecution ended, the Jewish strength never to give in turned against the guidance of rabbanim, so that obeying them feels like a prisoner's chains instead of a soldier's duty. An army sends its strongest men to the hardest front, so this generation was trusted with the hardest test. He brings R' Mendel of Rimanov's words that the last battle before Moshiach was pushed off by 150 years, and links it to the 1960s and the rise of personal technology, which, he says, even its own makers keep from their children. He tells stories of children harmed through simple phones, and teaches five rules for one who must use a device: who, when, what, where and how.

en: The speaker says that after outside persecution ended, the Jewish power never to give in was turned against following the rabbanim, so their guidance is felt as a prison instead of an army.
He argues that an army sends its strongest soldiers to the hardest front, so this generation's hard test is a sign that Heaven trusted it.
Personal technology, he says, entered quietly like the serpent's bite, and harms people's ability to think, focus and relate to others.
One whom Hashem requires to use a device for parnassah is like a soldier assigned to the nuclear department: he must go, but he must guard himself with great care.
He gives five rules for such use: who, when, what, where and how, and stresses the 'how' that children see at home.
There is no rule that a father may and his child may not; what a parent enjoys on a device, the children will learn to enjoy.

title.en: A generation led by gedolim, facing a test

summary.en: The speaker (not the Rav) speaks of the privilege of living in a generation with gedolim who lead it, says the idea of obeying them has been twisted, and describes the alarm over the new test of devices, even in Teaneck. He recalls how earlier generations struggled over Shabbos.

title.en: The yetzer hara's new tactic

summary.en: The speaker describes how easy Yiddishkeit is today, with Shabbos, kashrus and seforim all available. He says that once persecution ended, the yetzer hara turned the Jewish strength of not giving in against the young people's acceptance of their parents and rabbanim.

title.en: A soldier, not a prisoner

summary.en: The speaker contrasts a prison and an army, which look alike from outside, and says a Jew bound by the Torah should feel like a soldier, not an arrested man. He says young people answer every story with 'these are different times', and asks what kind of times they are.

title.en: The strongest are sent to the hardest front

summary.en: The speaker tells of a ba'al teshuvah who served in the Gulf War 'on the front' by washing laundry, and contrasts it with the elite soldiers sent after bin Laden. He concludes that Heaven sent this generation to the hardest front because it trusts it.

title.en: R' Mendel of Rimanov and Napoleon

summary.en: The speaker says the tzaddikim foresaw this generation, and brings what R' Shimon of Zhelichov wrote of R' Mendel of Rimanov, who wanted Napoleon to win while the Ba'al HaTanya opposed it, and who said before his passing that the last, hardest battle had been pushed off by 150 years. He links this to 1965 and the open breakdown of the street.

title.en: How technology crept in

summary.en: The speaker describes technology turning into a personal device, from the calculator to the car phone, and says the owners of the big technology companies send their children to schools without screens. He cites attention spans shrinking, and says a person emptied this way has no heart left for Shabbos.

title.en: Parnassah and the nuclear department

summary.en: The speaker takes up the claim that one has no choice for parnassah, says detailed guidelines go out of date quickly, and offers one clear approach: like soldiers who handle nuclear bombs, people carry devices that can destroy a whole home, even simple flip phones.

title.en: Stories of 'kosher' phones

summary.en: The speaker tells of a twelve-year-old boy in Monsey who was harmed by what a classmate showed him on the classmate's mother's talk-only phone, which the classmate had opened to the internet in minutes, and of a Boro Park menahel who found his own 'kosher' phone open to the internet. He says parents themselves often do not know.

title.en: When Hashem sends one into the job

summary.en: The speaker tells of a yungerman with many children who refused any job tied to the internet until his rav and a Rebbe in Monsey told him he must take one and guard himself. He compares this to a soldier ordered into the nuclear department, who goes as a hero and asks his son to say Tehillim for him.

title.en: Five rules: who, when, what, where, how

summary.en: The speaker lays out five rules for one who must use a device, says very few truly need a smartphone on their person, and stresses that even filtered email is a serious business tool, not a pleasure. He tells of a Boro Park yungerman who keeps his smartphone in the car and told his son he touches it only when he must.

title.en: What children learn, and the last battle

summary.en: The speaker says there is no rule that permits a father what is forbidden to his child, and tells of a mother whose 'harmless' smartphone her children watched her enjoy. He closes that the internet will get worse, that this is the last and hardest battle R' Mendel spoke of, and that with pride in using only what one must, this generation will greet Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: This recording is not a shiur of the Rav but a talk by R' Langer at a gathering on technology, urging the listeners to go against the current and adopt the rabbonim's resolutions on phones and the internet.

abstract.en: The whole recording is a talk by another speaker, R' Langer (per the catalog), given in the Mashgiach's presence at a gathering about technology before the Yamim Noraim. He asks why we pray for life and answers that life is for Hashem's sake; true life is shown by a bird that swims against the current. He tells of young men who already switched to kosher phones, brings the Avnei Nezer's reading of a father's duty to teach his son to swim, and stresses following the rabbonim, like a grafted branch that lives only while bound to the old one. He reads 'nokef etzba' as an acronym for modern devices, retells R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's words on zealotry, tells the parable of the monkey trap and his own decision to give up his phone, and closes by reading the main takanos on phones, computers and the internet.

en: R' Langer says one asks for life because life is meant to be lived for Hashem, who has the greatest nachas from souls in a low generation.
He brings the halachic sign that a bird swimming against the current is not a treifah, and says this is what life means: standing up against the current.
Citing the Avnei Nezer, he explains a father's duty to teach his son to swim as preparing the child not to drown in the waters of this world.
He stresses that the chain of the generations holds only as long as one stays bound to the rabbonim and follows them.
He relays the rabbonim's resolutions: a kosher phone is best, a smartphone only where needed for a livelihood and kept at work, and the internet only with a filter and a rav's guidance.

title.en: Why ask for life: going against the current

summary.en: R' Langer opens in the Mashgiach's presence, asks why we pray for life before the Yamim Noraim, and answers that life is for Hashem's sake. He brings the halachic sign that a bird which swims against the current is kosher and calls that true life.

title.en: Following the rabbonim on technology

summary.en: He tells of young men who switched to kosher phones, brings the Avnei Nezer on teaching a child to swim, the grafted branch, Pinchas's zealotry, the Gemara on R' Meir and R' Akiva, and a reading of 'nokef etzba' as modern devices. He retells R' Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's words on zealotry and a story of a filter expert's son.

title.en: The monkey trap and his own decision

summary.en: He tells how monkeys are caught because they will not let go of the rice in their fist, and says that for now one can still let go. He tells how he decided to give up his own phone and how a policeman let him off a ticket, and brings R' Yisrael Salanter on simply acting.

title.en: Jumping in together; the takanos

summary.en: Using the parsha of Amalek, he calls on everyone to jump in together and accept the resolutions, then reads the main takanos on kosher phones, smartphones for a livelihood, computers and the internet, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches Jewish women that the home, with its kedushah and the light of Shabbos, is in their hands, and that a smartphone, the fruit of the 'smart tree' of knowledge, brings tumah into it.

abstract.en: The Rav explains that Beis Yaakov is the Jewish home, and that Chazal call a wife 'the house'; Rav Hirsch reads the wife as a fruitful vine at the house's pillars. Sarah's tent had a cloud of Shechinah, blessing in the dough and a Shabbos lamp that burned all week. These left at her death and returned only with Rivka, because the merit of Avraham and Yitzchak was not enough: the woman is the spirit of the home and carries the light of Shabbos into the weekdays. Reb Zusha would not enter a house until the Biur was thrown out; so too a smartphone brings tumah that darkens the Shabbos lights. The tree of knowledge was a 'smart tree' bearing smartphones, and the women, whose mitzvos repair Chava's sin, are called on to clean their homes of it and build a holy Shabbos home.

en: Beis Yaakov is the Jewish home, and everything that happens in it, including the growth of the family, is entrusted to the akeres habayis, the woman of the house.
The cloud of Shechinah, the blessing in the dough and the Shabbos lamp left Sarah's tent at her death and returned only when Rivka came.
The woman is responsible for the kashrus of the home and brings in kedushah, tznius and the spirit of Shabbos, which continues into the weekdays and which a G-d-fearing visitor can feel.
A smartphone in the home brings in tumah and weekday darkness that contradict Shabbos and darken its lights.
The Rav calls on the women to clean their homes of the smartphone like chametz and to build a pure Shabbos home, lighting candles with tzedakah and tefillah for their husbands and children.

title.en: The Jewish home is in the woman's hands

summary.en: After brief announcements, the Rav opens with the passuk 'so shall you say to Beis Yaakov' and explains that Beis Yaakov is the Jewish home, which Chazal identify with the wife. He brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch on the wife as a fruitful vine at the pillars of the house, and describes Sarah's tent with its cloud, the blessing in the dough and the Shabbos lamp, all of which left at her death.

title.en: Why the blessings returned only with Rivka

summary.en: The Rav asks why the blessings left although Avraham and Yitzchak still lived there, and answers that their merit was not enough: only with Rivka, the akeres habayis, did the Shechinah return, for she is the spirit of the house. He explains that the woman brings kedushah, tznius and the spirit of Shabbos into the weekdays, which a G-d-fearing visitor senses, and reads 'her lamp does not go out at night' as the Shabbos light that stays lit all week.

title.en: Reb Zusha, the Biur and the smartphone

summary.en: The Rav tells how Reb Zusha stopped at the door of a house because he sensed tumah, and entered only after the host threw out Moshe Mendelssohn's Biur. He applies it to a smartphone, which brings tumah and weekday darkness into a Jewish home; on Friday night the good angel sighs at such a house and the evil angel rejoices, while a pure home raises children like olive saplings.

title.en: The 'smart tree' and the call to cleanse the home

summary.en: The Rav explains that women's mitzvos of challah, niddah and candle lighting repair Chava's sin of eating from the tree of knowledge, which he calls a 'smart tree' whose fruit were smartphones; a smartphone at home renews that sin and damages the bond with husband and children. He calls on the women to clean their homes of it like chametz, to light Shabbos candles with tzedakah and tefillah for husband and children, to welcome the good angel, and closes with brachos.

title.en: Second speaker: the lowest generation

summary.en: Another speaker, mostly in English, relates Rav Shimshon's question why the final generation is the lowest, and a Midrash about Yosef Meshisa, who entered the Beis HaMikdash for the Romans and then refused to go back in, dying like Rabbi Akiva. With a mashal of a father who finds his lost son, he explains that a generation far from Hashem that reaches out to Him attains a special level.

title.en: Three perspectives on digital technology

summary.en: The speaker presents three perspectives: not everyone will pass this test, as in past challenges such as Shabbos work in America and the exodus from Egypt; the technology was created by Hashem as a test specifically for Klal Yisrael; and technology is only at its beginning, so one must ask not what is wrong but what comes next.

title.en: Barzilai and inviting Hashem home

summary.en: Through Barzilai haGiladi, who was rewarded with a place at Shlomo HaMelech's table for taking in Dovid HaMelech in his time of need, the speaker says that Hashem, as it were, is desperate for people who will invite Him into their homes while the world is drawn to its devices.

title.en: Taking stock: need versus want

summary.en: The speaker urges families to take stock of their devices, filters and settings, with stories of parents who were too relaxed and of a boy who kept his filter so as not to influence others. He discusses using a device only out of need, seeing each new technology as a downgrade, and avoiding both extremes with children, and closes by recalling the mesirus nefesh of past generations.

title.en: Unity and following the chachamim

summary.en: A further speaker says the gathering itself is a kiddush Hashem and that unity forms clouds of glory. He tells of a talmid of the Avnei Nezer stranded among Cantonists on Shavuos, whose words on 'there you will be buried' his Rebbe valued: in later exile, not following the chachamim brings destruction.

title.en: Teaching children to swim; Gideon's three hundred

summary.en: The speaker brings the Gemara that a father must teach his son to swim, explained as keeping afloat against the currents of society, the Zohar that even one united congregation can bring the geulah, and the story of Gideon's three hundred who did not kneel to drink and with whom Hashem saved Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach on the pilgrims' shoes

summary.en: The speaker brings Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach's explanation of 'how beautiful are your steps in shoes': Hashem's greatest nachas comes from the hard journey up to Yerushalayim in shoes, more than from the joy inside the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Rav Meir Shapiro: his mother, Prague and Pressburg

summary.en: Stories of Rav Meir Shapiro: his mother weeping when no melamed awaited him after a move, which he called the source of the Daf Yomi idea, and his comparison of Prague, where he was shown only relics of Yiddishkeit, with Pressburg of the Chasam Sofer, who made no compromises.

title.en: The speaker's own phone; no test too great

summary.en: The speaker tells how meeting two former students whose homes were damaged by phones led him to give up his smartphone, how a police officer let him go without a ticket the morning after he decided, and a story of a Rebbe who knew a merchant's ship had not sunk because Hashem does not send a test a person cannot bear.

title.en: The chicken that was an eagle

summary.en: The speaker tells a mashal of the Vilkomir Maggid about an eagle hatched among chickens who discovered he could fly, applying it to Jews who forget they descend from the Avos and Imahos, and speaks of giving up conveniences as a korban, through which yeshuos come.

title.en: The takanos and closing wishes

summary.en: The speaker presents the takanos in the booklet: a kosher or basic phone is preferred, a smartphone only for parnassah, filtered and not used in public, and internet blocked at home. He encourages the women to strengthen one another and closes with wishes for a good year and the coming of Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how the Asarah Maamaros of creation were revealed through the Ten Makkos and given in the Aseres Hadibros, and how Nissan, the month of renewal and of emunah, and its matzah call on a person to renew himself.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the three upper and seven lower levels, which become more tangible as they descend into the world. Hashem created the world with the Asarah Maamaros, but no one saw it; through the Ten Makkos He showed that every part of creation is His, against idolatry and against philosophers who say He left the world to run by itself. The makkos went in reverse order, from earthly to heavenly, and the Torah, through the Aseres Hadibros, then contained it all. He turns to Nissan, the reishis of the year, when the world was actually created and everything is renewed, and says a person should renew himself in avodas Hashem. Avraham, the first Jew, gave the mitzvah of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah. Man contains all ten traits, so bread is his food; matzah, three times forty-five, stands higher than bread, three times twenty-six. He urges care with good matzos, since Nissan's reishis of mercy shields from Tishrei's judgment.

en: Hashem created the world with the Asarah Maamaros, and through the Ten Makkos He showed openly that every sphere of creation is in His hand.
The makkos refuted both idolatry, with a separate god for each force, and the philosophers' view that Hashem no longer runs the world; He watches over every detail.
Nissan is the reishis of the year, when the world was actually created and Hashem's renewal filters down into nature, and a person should use it to renew himself in avodas Hashem.
Pesach is the time of emunah: Avraham, the first Jew, gave the mitzvah of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah.
Matzah, three times forty-five, stands higher than bread, three times twenty-six, and a person should take care to have good matzos.

title.en: The Asarah Maamaros revealed in the Ten Makkos

summary.en: The Rav describes the three upper and seven lower levels, which grow more tangible as they descend and can be used for good or bad. He explains that through the Ten Makkos Hashem showed that He made the world with the Asarah Maamaros, against those who believe in a separate god for each force, and that the Torah, through the Aseres Hadibros, then contained it all.

title.en: Heavenly and earthly maamaros, makkos in reverse

summary.en: The Rav explains that Bereishis is the first maamar and the source of the others, followed by three heavenly and then earthly maamaros. The makkos went in reverse order, from the earth up to the heavens, to show against the philosophers that Hashem controls every detail; he notes the sets of seven and three, and mentions that the seder plate and the makkos are also arranged by the ten sefiros.

title.en: Nissan, the reishis and month of renewal

summary.en: The Rav explains that Nissan is the reishis: the world was conceived in Tishrei with judgment but actually created in Nissan with mercy, and the Jewish nation was formed then. Hashem's daily renewal of creation filters down in this month, and he describes how nature awakens in spring after the deadness of winter.

title.en: Renewing oneself in Nissan

summary.en: The Rav says a person should use Nissan to renew himself in avodas Hashem, and tells of a tzaddik who found it hard to take time to answer a question because an hour in Nissan equals a whole day. He asks why a person should lag behind a renewed world, brings the Navi's image of the dry bones rising, and says the new clothes and cleaned house of Pesach should move a person to ask how he himself can become new.

title.en: Avraham, emunah and matzah

summary.en: The Rav connects Nissan as reishis with Avraham Avinu, the first Jew, who gave the first mitzvah, emunah, which the Rambam counts first. Pesach is the time of emunah, and matzah, as the Zohar calls it, is the food of emunah; Avraham, the beginning, also ate matzah.

title.en: Animals, man and the food of man

summary.en: The Rav explains that each animal was created with one trait, so its behavior can be predicted, while man, to whom every part of creation contributed, holds all ten and each person has his own dominant traits. Bread is therefore the food of man, and he brings the passuk that man lives not by bread alone but by what comes from the mouth of Hashem.

title.en: The Shem Havayah, Shabbos, and matzah above bread

summary.en: The Rav divides the sefiros into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim, as seen in how tefillin straps are wound, and explains the Shem Havayah and its spelled-out form of ten letters. He connects reshus hayachid on Shabbos to Hashem, citing the Zohar, and shows that lechem is three times twenty-six while matzah is three times forty-five, so matzah is far higher.

title.en: Good matzos and the two reishis

summary.en: The Rav urges care to have good, guarded matzos, since on Pesach a person charges himself with emunah for the year. He explains that there are two reishis, Nissan with mercy and Tishrei with judgment, and one who puts himself under Nissan's authority need not fear Rosh Hashanah; the closing words on renewal are largely unintelligible.

oneLiner.en: The Rav strengthens his listeners in tefillah: davening is the service of the heart and a meeting with the King, to be done slowly, together, aloud, and without talking, especially during chazaras hashatz.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah': the teivah is the word, and each word of davening must be lit up with one's whole strength. His rebbe, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, explained that the world is a flood of apikorsus and desires, and the Jew is saved by entering the teivah of tefillah. The Rav recalls how loud, joyful davening by bachurim led to the founding of the Chevra Emunas Yisroel, and says davening needs constant chizuk because people treat it lightly. Tefillah is the service of the heart: it is a meeting with the King, which the Gemara calls pegiah. He tells of a simple Jew whose heartfelt Tehillim saved him from an informer. He then speaks sharply about leaving the room during chazaras hashatz and about talking in davening, and closes by asking for tefillah for the Jewish people in hard times.

en: Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the teivah of Noach is the word of tefillah, and one must put one's whole strength into each word.
Tefillah is the service of the heart; its essence is the heart's longing and kavanah, not only the spoken words or their translation.
Davening is speaking directly to Hashem and meeting Him; the Gemara's word pegiah means an appointment with the King.
To daven well one must daven slowly, so that the heart understands each word, and together with others who want to daven.
Chazaras hashatz, instituted by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, is a great opportunity, and walking out to chat during it is not fitting.
Talking during davening brings destruction, while not talking brings protection and blessing.

title.en: The teivah of the word of tefillah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah' as lighting up each word of davening. He cites Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz that the world is a flood of apikorsus and desires, and a Jew is saved by entering the teivah of tefillah; he adds that davening strengthens one against Amalek.

title.en: How the Chevra Emunas Yisroel began

summary.en: The Rav tells how bachurim davening loudly and with joy in a summer season led to a minyan in a store front in Boro Park, the start of the Chevra Emunas Yisroel. He says davening needs chizuk every few years, and brings the Gemara that people treat lightly the things that stand at the height of the world, which is tefillah.

title.en: Tefillah as the service of the heart

summary.en: From the Slonimer sefarim the Rav brings that the mitzvah of tefillah is 'to serve Him with all your heart', the service of the heart, while Torah is the service of the mind. The essence of tefillah is the heart, not speech; with the Chovos HaLevavos he defines it as the soul's longing for G-d, more than knowing the meaning of the words.

title.en: Standing before the King

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Berachos that tefillah three times a day comes from a passuk in Tehillim whose word he reads as the heart pouring out. Shemoneh Esrei is in the second person, spoken straight to Hashem; he cites the Rambam and Reb Chaim on knowing one stands before the King. He tells of one who davened mincha gedolah because his heart could not wait, and brings the words of Yedid Nefesh.

title.en: Moments of hispashtus and an appointment with the King

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shulchan Aruch that early chassidim reached hispashtus hagashmiyus in davening, and says simple people today can still merit moments of it. Pegiah means an appointment with the King of kings. He then explains how to work on it: davening slowly so the heart understands each word, and davening together with others, as Jews once used to.

title.en: The simple Jew and 'Tzam'ah nafshi'

summary.en: The Rav tells a story told by the Beis Avraham of Slonim: a simple Jew named Ephraim, threatened by an informer for selling brandy without a permit, went to shul to say Tehillim, and at 'Tzam'ah nafshi l'Elokim' forgot his trouble and longed only for Hashem; when the police came they found nothing. He concludes that davening together with achdus lets the heart pour out.

title.en: Ramban on davening aloud; an hour and a half

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo: the purpose of creation and of the mitzvos is that people acknowledge the Creator, and this is the purpose of raising the voice in tefillah and of the batei knesios. He then brings the Tanya in Iggeres HaKodesh that even working people should spend at least an hour and a half on shacharis.

title.en: Chazaras hashatz is not a break

summary.en: The Rav addresses a new problem: young men walk out into the hall to chat during chazaras hashatz. He explains its greatness, instituted by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, brings the Mishnah Berurah about following in an open siddur, and says the coffee room is part of the beis medrash; he brings the Tosfos Yom Tov that the decrees of Tach v'Tat came because of talking during davening.

title.en: The Skverer fire, the late soul, and a closing plea

summary.en: The Rav tells that when the Skverer Rebbe's beis medrash burned, only the room where no one talked during davening remained, and speaks of the Tosfos Yom Tov's Mi Sheberach. He tells of a soul that came too late for a tikkun because in life it came late to davening and learning. He closes saying the tzibur davens well, and asks for tefillah for the Jewish people and the world in a time of trouble, and for Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: At Kever Rachel, the Rav explains that Rachel is the mother who carries the Jewish souls through exile until they are handed over to Yaakov, and that Jewish tears in exile carry great weight.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk that Yaakov saw Rachel and the sheep of Lavan and rolled the stone off the well, and asks why the two are joined. Rachel, he explains, is the mother of the Jews in exile, who arouses mercy for them; Lavan's sheep were Jewish souls captive in Lavan's kelipah, and a Midrash counts Yaakov's six hundred thousand sheep as the souls he later refined in Mitzrayim. Seeing both, Yaakov wished to lighten their exile and rolled a stone off the heart of Knesses Yisrael. Since the souls were not yet ready, he worked seven years for Rachel and they stayed meanwhile with her. When Yaakov reached Eretz Yisrael her task ended, she died and was buried on the way, to resume it in later exiles. At Kever Rachel the Rav asks that the time come for Rachel to bring the flock to Yaakov, tells of the river of Jewish tears seen by the Sadigura Rebbe, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

en: Yaakov rolled the stone because of two things together: Rachel and the sheep of Lavan.
Rachel is the mother of the Jews in exile, whose task is to revive them, comfort them and weep for them.
Lavan's sheep were Jewish souls held captive in Lavan's kelipah, which Yaakov would later refine into the six hundred thousand souls of Klal Yisrael.
Because the souls were not yet ready, Yaakov worked seven years for Rachel, and meanwhile the flock stayed with her.
Rachel died when Yaakov reached Eretz Yisrael and was buried on the way, so that she could resume her task when the Jews would go out again into exile.
Jewish tears in exile have great importance; they are the tears of Rachel.

title.en: Seven years with Rachel, then burial on the way

summary.en: The Rav explains the rolled stone as easing the heart of Knesses Yisrael, and why Yaakov worked seven years for Rachel while the souls stayed with her. Her task ended when Yaakov reached Eretz Yisrael, so she died and was buried on the way for later exiles; the shepherds' words that Rachel comes with the sheep meant the time had come to hand them to Yaakov.

title.en: At Kever Rachel: tears and tefillah

summary.en: Standing at Kever Rachel, the Rav asks that the time come for Rachel to bring the flock to Yaakov and the Jews to Eretz Yisrael, stresses the worth of Jewish tears in exile with the story of the Sadigura Rebbe seeing the Ruzhiner at a river of tears, and closes with a tefillah for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At Kever Rochel on the last day of Av, the Rav explains Elul as the month Yaakov 'grabbed' back from Esav, traces the power of grabbing to Rochel's self-giving and to Binyamin, and calls for grabbing oneself out of today's trials through Torah together with tefillah.

abstract.en: Speaking at Kever Rochel as Av ends, the Rav brings the Zohar that Yaakov 'grabbed' the month of Elul from Esav, and a Midrash about a maiden who grabbed an angel's wings and was set as Elul's mazal, Besulah. Since a mazal is the flow of influence on its month, Elul's influence is grabbing: a person should grab from the sitra achra, not be grabbed by it. He then turns to Rochel, whose soul left with Binyamin's birth, and to the Midrash where Hashem forgives Israel in the merit of her giving her signs to her sister. Binyamin, her quintessence, has the power to grab back, as on Tu B'Av when his tribe grabbed wives at Shiloh. Sitting at Rochel's grave, the Rav calls for a resolution not to be grabbed by the yetzer hara, laments young men caught by electronic devices, and insists that Torah and tefillah must go together, recommending Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah before Shabbos davening.

en: Following the Zohar, the Rav explains that Elul is a month Yaakov grabbed for himself from Esav's portion.
A mazal is the source of influence that flows onto its month, so the influence of Elul is the power to grab: to take from the sitra achra rather than be taken by it.
Rochel's soul left together with Binyamin's birth, so Binyamin is the quintessence of his mother.
Tu B'Av became a day of grabbing through Binyamin, whose tribe grabbed wives at Shiloh, and from then on Yaakov's portion can be grabbed back.
The Rav says Torah and tefillah must go together, and that this is the only counsel for the trials of our time.

title.en: Kever Rochel and the grabbed month of Elul

summary.en: The Rav opens at Kever Rochel, saying the whole area is Rochel's place, and speaks of Rochel as mother of the Jewish people. He brings the Zohar that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav and that Yaakov went and grabbed Elul.

title.en: The mazal of Elul and the power to grab

summary.en: The Rav brings a Midrash that a maiden grabbed the wings of one of the fallen angels, flew up to the Kisei HaKavod and was set as the mazal Besulah, the mazal of Elul. He explains that a mazal is the flow of influence on its month, so Elul's influence is grabbing: a person must grab from the sitra achra and not let himself be grabbed by the desires of the times.

title.en: Rochel's passing, Binyamin and her plea

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rochel's soul left as Binyamin was born, and since the moment of passing holds the essence of a whole life, Binyamin is her quintessence. He brings the Midrash in which the Avos and Moshe pleaded in vain and Hashem forgave Israel for Rochel, who gave her signs to her sister, and the passuk promising that her children will return. Because Binyamin carries her self-giving, he has the merit to grab back what Esav wants for himself, since all of creation belongs to Yisrael.

title.en: Binyamin grabs: Tu B'Av and Kislev

summary.en: The Rav tells of the war with Binyamin, the oath not to give them wives, and the advice to grab the daughters dancing at Shiloh, as in Sefer Shoftim; this was on Tu B'Av, which the Gemara counts as a yom tov for this reason. He explains that from Tu B'Av on the portion is Yaakov's, that the day became a day of grabbing through Binyamin, and that Binyamin's month Kislev also grabs days of Teves for Chanukah.

title.en: A resolution at Rochel's grave as Av ends

summary.en: On the last day of Av, sitting at the grave of Rochel, the root of grabbing, the Rav calls for a resolution not to let the yetzer hara grab, which he calls the avodah of Elul that Yaakov began. He laments the fine young men who come to him caught by today's electronic devices, says breaking out takes real self-sacrifice, and that everyone is affected to some degree.

title.en: Torah together with tefillah

summary.en: The Rav says that one cannot have tefillah without Torah nor Torah without tefillah, and tells of a young man who came crying to the Satmar Rav that he could not rid himself of bad thoughts. He stresses that no one can be sure when a sudden trial will come, that Torah with tefillah is the only counsel, and calls on all to enter the grabbed month of Elul grabbing with Torah and good middos, not foolishness.

title.en: Good davening and Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah

summary.en: The Rav calls good davening the best counsel and recalls great men who came to tefillah with deep seriousness, naming Rabbi Shlomo Heiman, Rabbi Yisrael Chaim Kaplan and Rabbi Reuven Grozovsky. He speaks of chevlei Moshiach, says Rebbe Elimelech nullified them through tefillah, and recommends saying Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah on Shabbos morning before davening, taking ten minutes to plead before Hashem.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 3, the Rav explains how Chochmah and Binah give birth to love and fear of Hashem, and how Da'as, deep and lasting concentration, makes those middos genuine and lasting.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the weeks of Sefirah, when the middos are refined, since good middos are the prerequisite for Torah. He then reads Tanya chapter 3: the soul has intellect (Chochmah, Binah, Da'as) and middos, and the intellect is the father and mother of the middos, with Da'as as the bridge that controls them; a bowl of cookies and a gifted child who is not yet responsible illustrate this. Chochmah is the flash of insight, Binah builds it up like bricks. Contemplating Hashem's greatness first produces yirah, a sense of shame before His greatness, and only afterwards true ahavah, the soul's thirst to cling to Hashem. A digression on Shechem and Dina explains the fiery words of love. Finally, Da'as means intense and lengthy concentration; without it love and fear are only empty imaginings. He ends with refining the middos through Sefirah.

en: Chochmah and Binah are the father and mother of the middos, and Da'as is the bridge that unites intellect with emotion and controls it.
Chochmah is a sudden flash of new insight whose origin a person does not know; Binah builds on it thought by thought until a complete structure stands.
Although ahavah ranks higher than yirah, in attaining them yirah must come first; genuine ahavah follows as a gift from Hashem.
True yirah is not fear of punishment but shame before Hashem's greatness, that so small a creature should go against His will.
Ahavah is the soul's yearning to cling to Hashem, like the fire in the heart that thirsts for the water of Chochmah.
Da'as is strong and lengthy concentration on Hashem's greatness; without it, love and fear are only imaginings.

title.en: Sefirah, middos and the text of chapter 3

summary.en: The Rav explains that middos are refined during Sefirah because they are the prerequisite for Torah, and links each chapter of Pirkei Avos to that week's middah. He then reads Tanya chapter 3: the soul is divided into intellect, Chochmah, Binah and Da'as, and middos, which are born of the intellect.

title.en: Da'as as the bridge: cookies and a katan

summary.en: Chochmah and Binah give birth to the middos, and Da'as is the bridge that unites them. With a jar of cookies the Rav shows how understanding produces desire and how Da'as, responsibility, holds it in check; a child may be a genius but is not yet a bar da'as.

title.en: Chochmah as a flash, Binah as building

summary.en: Applied to avodas Hashem, seeing and contemplating Hashem's greatness gives birth to love or fear. The Rav defines the intellect as the power in the mind that produces thought: Chochmah, koach mah, is a sudden flash of insight from Hashem, and Binah, from binyan, builds it brick by brick into a complete understanding.

title.en: Birchas Yotzer: fear, then love

summary.en: The Rav shows the birth of the middos in davening: in Birchas Yotzer one contemplates the greatness of creation and produces yirah, then in Ahavah Rabbah the great love of Hashem for Klal Yisroel arouses love in return, leading to the self-sacrifice of Krias Shema. This requires thinking deeply, not running through the words.

title.en: Why yirah must come before ahavah

summary.en: Though ahavah is the higher middah, genuine love can only come after fear. Fear is within a person's choice, love is not, as the spinach example shows; once a person has yirah, Hashem grants ahavah, the 'avodas matanah'. The Rav brings the Maggid's words on the way of the 'ish' and a Gemara that yirah first is a good sign.

title.en: Higher fear is shame before greatness

summary.en: The Tanya begins with the higher fear of Hashem's greatness, not the lower fear of punishment. The Rav compares it to everyone rising when a president enters, and brings the Gemara that yirah is busha, shame, and the reading of Bereishis as 'yarei boshes'. After the fear the heart flames with love.

title.en: The words of love by Shechem and Dina

summary.en: The four expressions of love in the Tanya appear in the parsha of Shechem and Dina. The Rav explains that Shechem carried sparks of kedushah: he and Dina were reincarnated as Zimri and Kozbi and later as Rabbi Akiva and his wife, and their daughter became Osnas, Yosef's wife. The fierce words of love reflect those sparks struggling to break free of the klipah.

title.en: Love as the soul's thirst

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav says every Jew who unites his Chochmah and Binah can come to a burning love for Hashem, klos hanefesh, like a thirsty man in the desert who sees water. The fire in the heart thirsts for the water of Chochmah, the point of G-dliness in the soul; the other middos are branches of love and fear.

title.en: Da'as: intense and lasting focus

summary.en: Da'as, from 'yada', means connecting: to give birth one must fix the mind with strength and for a long time on Hashem's greatness, or the love and fear will be only empty imaginings. Da'as sustains the middos. The Rav closes on purifying the middos during Sefirah, comparing the last weeks to refining silver to sterling.

oneLiner.en: At the place of Shmuel Hanavi, the Rav explains why it is a place of Rosh Hashanah: here Chana's long tefillah was answered, she first called Hashem by the name Tzevaos, and Shmuel, the head of the prophets, was born.

abstract.en: The Rav suggests that just as each place in Eretz Yisroel is tied to a mitzvah, the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is conceived, since here Chana conceived Shmuel. Many laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, among them standing before the King. Eli did not know that a long tefillah is a merit, which Chana introduced; the Rav adds that tefillah is something people belittle. He brings a Midrash that one can be barren in tefillah and in Torah, and says this place is a segulah for whoever finds learning and davening hard. Shmuel's first prophecy punished Chofni and Pinchas, who kept women from returning to their families. Chana was the first to use the name Tzevaos, which the Rav explains as the hosts of Jewish souls. Citing the Chasam Sofer, he says Chana's tefillah was on Rosh Hashanah, and closes with a brachah for a fruitful year.

en: The Rav suggests that the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is conceived, because Chana conceived Shmuel there.
Many laws of tefillah, including standing before the King in Shemoneh Esrei, are learned from Chana.
Eli objected to Chana's long tefillah because he did not know that lengthening one's tefillah is a merit, something Chana introduced.
The Rav says this place is a segulah for one who finds davening and learning hard, so that his Torah and tefillah bear fruit.
Chana was the first to call Hashem 'Tzevaos', and she used it to ask for children; the Rav explains Tzevaos as the hosts of Jewish souls.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav says Chana's tefillah took place on Rosh Hashanah, which is why it is the haftarah of Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: The place of Shmuel as a place of Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav mentions the segulah of being called up for the Rosh Hashanah haftarah, and suggests that just as places in Eretz Yisroel are tied to mitzvos, the place of Shmuel Hanavi is tied to Rosh Hashanah, the day the world is conceived, since Chana conceived Shmuel here.

title.en: Laws of tefillah learned from Chana

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that many laws of tefillah come from Chana, such as standing before the King. He describes Eli's impatience with her long davening and explains that Eli did not know that a long tefillah is a merit, adding that tefillah is among the things people belittle.

title.en: Barren in tefillah and Torah; a segulah here

summary.en: The Rav cites the Chasam Sofer on the segulah of the Rosh Hashanah maftir and a Midrash that one can be barren in tefillah and in Torah. He says the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a segulah for whoever struggles to daven and learn, and recalls that Chana's tefillah brought Shmuel, the head of the prophets.

title.en: Chofni and Pinchas, and the name Tzevaos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shmuel's first prophecy was a punishment of Chofni and Pinchas, who delayed the women's offerings and kept them from their families. He then notes that the name Tzevaos first appears in Chana's tefillah, ties it to netzach and hod, and explains it as the hosts of Jewish souls, so that this is a place to be helped with children and with fruit in Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Chana's tefillah was on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav shows from the word 'vehaya' and from the Chasam Sofer on 'miyamim yamimah' that Chana davened on Rosh Hashanah, when Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh. Those at this place take on the aspect of Rosh Hashanah, of Chana and of Shmuel, and he closes with a brachah for a bright, fruitful year.

summary.en: A niggun is sung, followed by a brief remark recalling that the niggun was sung in camp in the days of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim about to learn in Eretz Yisroel, the Rav explains that being in the land is not enough: one must be 'planted' in it, feel its holiness every day as on Rosh Hashanah, and keep one's dirah a holy place.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a story of a sick tzaddik who asked a traveler to Eretz Yisroel to sip water for him, since one who prepares to go is already 'Eretz Yisroel'. Addressing bachurim going to learn there, he warns that one can be in the land without being in it, as people walk the streets on Shabbos with no tie to Shabbos; Eretz Yisroel is the Shabbos of the world, and one must be planted in it like a tree, not lie there like a log. Every mitzvah and every sin there is multiplied. From the Ruzhiner and the passuk 'from the beginning of the year' he shows that Eretz Yisroel is a constant Rosh Hashanah. He brings the Chasam Sofer, the great tzaddikim who were not allowed to go, the Torah beginning and ending with the land, the Hafla'ah and Chasam Sofer on Moshe's tefillah, and the diamond parable of 'a good and wide land'. He closes by asking the bachurim to keep their dirah holy, with rules for sleep and order.

en: One can go to Eretz Yisroel and still not be in Eretz Yisroel; being there requires zechus and a real connection to the land.
Eretz Yisroel is the Shabbos of the world, and a mitzvah or a sin done there weighs far more than elsewhere.
A Jew in Eretz Yisroel must be planted there like a tree, with love of the land and awareness of its responsibility, not lie there like a cut log.
Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah: in it a person is judged every day, so every day there must be lived with the seriousness of Rosh Hashanah.
One must not grow accustomed to Eretz Yisroel; it should feel new each day, as Torah should.
The bachurim's dirah in Eretz Yisroel should be holy, with rules for curfew and enough sleep so they can daven and learn with a fresh mind.

title.en: Going to Eretz Yisroel, but being there?

summary.en: The Rav tells of a sick tzaddik who drank water from the mouth of a traveler to Eretz Yisroel, then addresses bachurim going there to learn. Citing the meraglim, he warns that one can go to the land without being in it, and calls Eretz Yisroel the Shabbos of geography.

title.en: Planted, not a log

summary.en: From 'plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance' the Rav gives the parable of a log that does not blossom in spring because it was never planted. He compares Eretz Yisroel to Shabbos, where every mitzvah, and every sin, counts many times over.

title.en: Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Ruzhiner asked a man leaving for Eretz Yisroel whether he could live every day as Rosh Hashanah, and explains that in Eretz Yisroel one is judged daily because the land was created first. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the land makes a tzaddik greater and a rasha worse, laments idle bachurim there, and quotes the Chasam Sofer on giving one's soul to rise to the land.

title.en: A zechus earlier generations lacked

summary.en: The Rav says the Torah of Eretz Yisroel is a different kind of Torah, contrasts today's overnight flight with the mesirus nefesh of earlier travelers, and notes that the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon and the Chofetz Chaim were held back from going while this generation is allowed. He then brings Rashi that the Torah opens with Bereishis to show the land belongs to the Jews.

title.en: Immersing before entering the land

summary.en: The Rav shows that the last words Moshe wrote in the Torah speak of the land, so the Torah begins and ends with Eretz Yisroel. He brings a tzaddik's teaching that water surrounds the land on four sides so one immerses before entering, and warns that the Satan invests there, as seen in the machlokes and pashkevilim on Yerushalayim's walls.

title.en: Kiddush, and Moshe's tefillah in the land

summary.en: The Rav compares the light of Eretz Yisroel to the holiness of Shabbos and of a tzaddik's kiddush, recalling the Satmar Rebbe's kiddush. He then brings the Hafla'ah that Moshe prayed to be able to pray, and the Chasam Sofer's answer why Moshe did not say this during his forty days in heaven: the ground of Eretz Yisroel is holier than the heaven above chutz la'aretz.

title.en: A diamond the size of a walnut

summary.en: The Rav asks how the small land can be called 'wide' and answers with the parable of a costly plot in Manhattan versus a diamond the size of a walnut. He describes feeling every step there, and from Rashi on 'and He gives it to you' teaches that one must not grow accustomed to the land, just as Torah must feel new each day.

title.en: The dirah that was a kiddush Hashem

summary.en: The Rav says a bachur who goes with good intentions and stays away from parties and machlokes can feel the different light in learning, davening and Shabbos. He recalls that the bachurim's dirah in Yerushalayim was known as a refined place, a kiddush Hashem, and notes he heard it has recently declined, with late nights and idle talk.

title.en: Takanos for a holy dirah

summary.en: The Rav asks the bachurim to renew the old standard: rules for a curfew, quiet and seven or eight hours of sleep, so they can daven properly and learn with a fresh mind. A Jew's home should feel like Shabbos, with the Shechinah in it, and he closes with a brachah for the holiness of Eretz Yisroel.

catalogTitle: שלשה לבושים לנפש אלקות - מחשבה' דיבור' ד ומעשה. חב"ד- השגת התורה' אהבה' יראה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's teaching that the G-dly soul is clothed in the thought, speech and deed of the 613 mitzvos, with its intellect clothed in Torah study and its love and fear of Hashem as the roots of the positive and negative commandments.

abstract.en: The Rav learns Tanya chapter four: besides its ten faculties, the G-dly soul has three garments, thought, speech and deed. Following the Arizal, every Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in these three ways; they weave his garment in Gan Eden and correspond to his limbs, and a mitzvah never done is a missing limb, while Gehinnom only washes off sins. What cannot be done in deed must at least be learned and spoken about. Intellect is clothed in grasping the Pardes of Torah, each person according to the root of his soul, illustrated with the Vilna Gaon and with the Beis Yosef at the Arizal's shiurim. Love is the root of the positive commandments and fear of the negative ones, as the Ramban explains. The 248 mitzvos are the 'limbs of the King'; a human organ is truly an eye or a heart only when it serves Hashem, as the Midrash of the donkey without a heart shows. He closes by distinguishing fear of punishment from the higher fear of shame before Hashem's greatness.

en: Besides its ten faculties, the G-dly soul has three garments, thought, speech and deed, and every Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in all three.
Mitzvos a person cannot do in deed he must at least learn and speak about; a mitzvah never fulfilled at all is a missing limb of the soul.
The intellect of the soul is clothed in grasping the Pardes of Torah, each person according to his ability and the root of his soul.
Love of Hashem is the root of the 248 positive commandments and fear of Hashem the root of the 365 prohibitions.
The 248 mitzvos are the 'limbs of the King', and a person's limbs are made to receive the corresponding heavenly powers.
True fear of Hashem is not fear of punishment but shame before His greatness.

title.en: Three garments of the G-dly soul

summary.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter four: beyond the ten faculties learned before, the G-dly soul has three garments, thought, speech and deed. He brings the Arizal that every Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in all three, and explains that they form the garment of the soul in Gan Eden, the 'chaluka d'rabbanan' mentioned before putting on the tallis.

title.en: The barefoot father and the missing limb

summary.en: The Rav tells of a great sage who appeared to his son in a dream in a wonderful garment but barefoot, because he had never collected tzedakah for the poor. He explains that the 613 mitzvos correspond to a person's limbs: Gehinnom only washes off the stain of a sin, but a mitzvah never done leaves a limb missing and requires coming back to the world.

title.en: Mitzvos one cannot perform

summary.en: The Rav asks what a person does with mitzvos he cannot perform, such as when his firstborn is a daughter or there is no Beis HaMikdash, and answers that he must at least think and speak about them by learning them; only one whom Heaven deems unable is excused. He then reads the Tanya's words on fulfilling the mitzvos in deed and studying their meaning and halachos in speech.

title.en: The orchard of Torah: Pardes

summary.en: The Rav explains that the intellect is clothed in grasping the 'Pardes' of Torah, its four layers of pshat, remez, drush and sod, likening it to a miner who digs beneath a beautiful field. He criticizes those who shy away from sod out of fear of greater responsibility, citing that one who keeps the first three and leaves out sod is called a 'pered', a mule.

title.en: Each according to the root of his soul

summary.en: The Rav explains that each person grasps Torah according to his capacity and the root of his soul, which can ascend through nefesh, ruach and neshamah, but some are rooted lower, like an inverted tree whose roots are in heaven. He illustrates with the Vilna Gaon, whom Reb Chaim of Volozhin could not equal, with the Beis Yosef who fell asleep at the Arizal's shiurim on sod, and adds that a person's intelligence also limits how far he can reach.

title.en: Love and fear as roots of the mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav reads that the soul's Chabad is clothed in Torah study and its emotions, love and fear, in the mitzvos: love is the root of the positive commandments and fear of the prohibitions. He brings the Ramban on zachor and shamor and the Gemara's rule that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition, and explains that a mitzvah done without love, like tefillin put on by rote, withers like a cut flower, though every Jew has a hidden love.

title.en: The limbs of the King and the heartless donkey

summary.en: The Rav reads that the 248 positive mitzvos are the 'limbs of the King' and explains that Hashem, who has no body, emanates 248 powers that come down as human limbs. He then tells the Midrash of the lion who killed the donkey that demanded a toll, and the fox who ate its heart and claimed it never had one, ending with 'kaved lev Paroh'.

title.en: An eye that sees, a heart that fears

summary.en: The Rav explains 'b'tzelem Elokim': each human organ is a receiver of a heavenly power, so the eye is called ayin because Hashem's 'seeing' is drawn into it, and a guarded eye becomes a chariot for that holiness; the heart corresponds to the heavenly heart of the thirty-two paths. An organ that does not serve Hashem, a heart without fear of Him or a knee that does not bow, is not truly that organ, which explains the Midrash about Pharaoh's heart.

title.en: Fear of punishment and fear of shame

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes the lower fear of punishment, which is fear for oneself, from the true fear of shame before Hashem's greatness, illustrated by how no one would do something disgusting in front of a president. He brings the Gemara that 'His fear upon your faces' means shame, mentions Yechezkel's vision of the 'Adam' above and its counterpart in the Sitra Achra, and ends where the next passage begins.

oneLiner.en: Opening his study of Shir Hashirim, the Rav explains why this song of love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael belongs to Shlomo HaMelech alone, and who Shlomo was: the king whose days and whose Beis HaMikdash were a foretaste of the time of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by asking why Shir Hashirim is called 'asher liShlomo', belonging to Shlomo, and answers that no one else could carry the song of love between Hashem and Klal Yisrael in both directions. It is a song of love, which is why it is said on Shabbos and why the Sfas Emes ties it to Pesach; it has no plain meaning and must be read only as a mashal. Song comes from feeling loved, and Shlomo, called Yedidyah, was so united with Hashem that his name became the name of the King of peace. The song is kodesh kodashim like the place of the keruvim, and Shlomo said it the day he finished the Beis HaMikdash, a day like Shemini Atzeres and the days of Moshiach. Its destruction on Tisha B'Av was tied to Shlomo, who returned as Yirmiyahu and will again become Shlomo. The Rav ends with Shlomo's unmatched wisdom and his role as Hashem's poet.

en: Shir Hashirim is 'asher liShlomo': it belongs to Shlomo, since only he could convey the song of love from Hashem to Klal Yisrael and back.
Shir Hashirim is a song of love, which is why it fits Shabbos and Pesach, the days of love.
Shir Hashirim has no plain meaning; one rises at once above the mashal of chosson and kallah to the nimshal.
Shir Hashirim is kodesh kodashim because, like the Holy of Holies with its keruvim, it is the place of the chosson and kallah.
Shlomo said Shir Hashirim on the day he completed the Beis HaMikdash, the dwelling of the chosson and kallah, and his era was a foretaste of the days of Moshiach.
Tisha B'Av is the opposite of Shemini Atzeres, and the soul of Shlomo who built the Beis HaMikdash returned as Yirmiyahu who saw its destruction.

title.en: Why the song is 'asher liShlomo'

summary.en: The Rav notes that unlike 'shir hamaalos leDavid', Shir Hashirim says 'asher liShlomo', and explains that the song belongs to Shlomo, since no one else could carry the love song between Hashem and Klal Yisrael in both directions. Therefore, before learning it, one should come to know who Shlomo was.

title.en: A song of love for Shabbos and Pesach

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shir Hashirim is a song of love and therefore said on Shabbos, a day of love without a korban chatas, and on Pesach, the Yom Tov of Avraham and chesed, as the Sfas Emes says. It has no plain meaning, only remez, drush and sod, and singing it requires the contentment of knowing one is loved.

title.en: Love that brings song; Shlomo the beloved

summary.en: The Rav shows that song flows from love: the angels, Klal Yisrael at the Yam Suf, and the Chareidim's Yedid Nefesh. Shlomo, beloved of Hashem and named Yedidyah, was so united with Hashem in love that 'Shlomo' in Shir Hashirim means both Shlomo HaMelech and the King to whom peace belongs.

title.en: Kodesh kodashim and the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Akiva's words that Shir Hashirim is kodesh kodashim and explains them through the Holy of Holies, where the two keruvim are chosson and kallah. Shlomo said Shir Hashirim on the day he finished the Beis HaMikdash, which is called a kallah, the home of the chosson and kallah.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the point in the middle

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shemini Atzeres is the climax of the year: all the Yomim Tovim circle around it, and it is the complete yichud of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, alone without the nations, a sample of the days of Moshiach. Its ushpiz is Shlomo HaMelech.

title.en: Shlomo's era, a foretaste of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem has not yet had full nachas from His world, as the Midrash on 'yismach Hashem bemaasav' says, and no person has ever reached all he wished, except Shlomo, of whom it says he achieved everything he desired. He then tells that on the morning after the Beis HaMikdash was completed Shlomo slept late, and the destruction was decreed.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, Yirmiyahu and Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tisha B'Av is the opposite of Shemini Atzeres, and that Shlomo, who built the Beis HaMikdash and wrote Shir Hashirim, returned as Yirmiyahu, who saw its destruction and wrote Eichah. Masechta Taanis ends with Chamishah Asar B'Av and the passuk 'tze'enah ur'enah... bamelech Shlomo', since in the future Yirmiyahu will again become Shlomo and sing Shir Hashirim.

title.en: Shlomo's greatness in Tanach

summary.en: The Rav shows that 'Shlomo HaMelech', eight letters, is tied to Shemini Atzeres, and its spelled-out letters equal Tisha B'Av in gematria. He then reads the pesukim in Melachim about Shlomo's kingdom, his peace and his rule from Tifsach to Azah, and contrasts the conquerors who took the world by war with Shlomo, who won it with wisdom.

title.en: Shlomo's wisdom and his song

summary.en: The Rav describes Shlomo's peace without the sword, his wisdom beyond all others as the Midrash explains the names in the passuk, and the fifteen generations from Avraham to Shlomo like the full moon. He concludes that of Shlomo's three seforim Shir Hashirim is the highest, since Hashem appointed him as His poet to carry the songs between the chosson and the kallah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Shir Hashirim is the 'holy of holies' and the crowning tenth song: it shows that even the bond of chassan and kallah in this world can be raised to holiness, and it was written by Shlomo HaMelech to console Klal Yisrael in galus with the promise of their closeness to Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's introduction: Shlomo HaMelech foresaw the exiles and wrote Shir Hashirim as the song of a 'living widow' longing for her Beloved. He recalls that every 'Shlomo' in the sefer also means Hashem, and explains Rabbi Akiva's statement that Shir Hashirim is holy of holies with a pshat of Reb Feivel on the olah and the shelamim: a Jew, whose body is of kelipas nogah, can sanctify worldly things, and Shir Hashirim reveals this by using the love of chassan and kallah as its mashal. He then shows that among the ten songs, and in every set of ten in the Torah, the tenth is tied to chassan and kallah. Shlomo, the fifteenth generation and the full moon, knew the decline would follow and wrote the sefer as a consolation for the galus. The Rav explains why Shir Hashirim has no pshat, why it belongs to Shlomo, and reads 'Yishakeini' as dveikus of spirit with spirit, which Klal Yisrael prefers to the 'wine' of the seventy nations.

en: Shlomo HaMelech foresaw the long galus and wrote Shir Hashirim so that Klal Yisrael, like a 'living widow' whose husband is far away, would remember their first closeness and know Hashem has not abandoned them.

A gentile can bring only an olah, which goes entirely to Heaven, while a Jew can bring a shelamim that is eaten, because a Jew can sanctify worldly acts; Shir Hashirim, by using the love of chassan and kallah as its mashal, shows that this world too can be elevated.
Of the ten songs, Shir Hashirim is ninth in time but tenth in importance, and in every set of ten in the Torah the tenth is connected with chassan and kallah.
Shlomo was the fifteenth generation from Avraham, the full moon of Klal Yisrael; knowing the decline would begin after him, he wrote Shir Hashirim as a consolation for the darkness of galus.
Unlike every other passuk, Shir Hashirim has no pshat; the Rav says it may not be learned according to its literal meaning, and the early commentators explained it entirely by sod.
'Yishakeini' expresses dveikus of spirit with spirit, the bond Klal Yisrael has with Hashem and holds dearer than all the 'wine' of the seventy nations.
