title.en: Rashi's introduction: the living widow

summary.en: The Rav reads Rashi's introduction: Shlomo foresaw exile after exile and wrote Shir Hashirim in the voice of a 'living widow' longing for her Beloved, so Klal Yisrael would know Hashem has not abandoned them. He recalls from the previous week that the sefer is a dialogue between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, and that 'Shlomo' means both the king and the King of peace.

title.en: Holy of holies: olah, shelamim and this world

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Akiva's words that Shir Hashirim is holy of holies, and explains them with Reb Feivel's pshat on the Midrash of north and south: a gentile can only bring an olah, a Jew can bring a shelamim, because a Jew's body is of kelipas nogah and can be sanctified. Shir Hashirim uses the love of chassan and kallah as its mashal and so shows that this world can be elevated, and he adds Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's mashal of the king who asked the baker for one pure loaf.

title.en: The tenth song and chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Targum's list of ten songs, in which Shir Hashirim is ninth, and explains that by importance it is the tenth, as order in time and order in importance can differ. He shows that the tenth of the ten maamaros, of the ten dibros and of Avraham's ten trials (the Akeidah, which brought about Yitzchak's zivug) is each tied to chassan and kallah, and so is Shir Hashirim.

title.en: The king's songs and the full moon

summary.en: The Rav brings a mashal of a king who sent away his queen: they exchanged songs, and their wise child joined them into one song, Shir Hashirim, which opens with the queen's praise of the king. He then explains that Knesses Yisrael is the moon receiving light from the sun, which waxes until the fifteenth of the month, and therefore the main Yomim Tovim fall on the fifteenth, while Shavuos is the continuation of Pesach.

title.en: Shlomo, the fifteenth generation

summary.en: Following the Midrash, Shlomo is the fifteenth generation from Avraham, the fullness of the moon, and the decline down to Tzidkiyahu and the churban begins after him. Knowing this, he wrote Shir Hashirim as a consolation for Jews in galus, just as he prepared a hidden chamber under the Beis HaMikdash where Yoshiyahu later hid the aron.

title.en: Pshat, drash and why Shir Hashirim has no pshat

summary.en: The Rav describes commentators, especially the Ibn Ezra, who sought pshat even against Chazal, and relates a saying comparing Rashi, the Ibn Ezra and the Ramban. He explains that while every passuk has a pshat, Shir Hashirim has none and may not be learned literally; the early commentators, including the Ramban's commentary, explained it entirely by sod.

title.en: Yishakeini: the kiss as dveikus

summary.en: The Rav begins the first passuk, where Knesses Yisrael sings to Hashem, and brings Rashi that she says it in galus and widowhood, longing for the closeness of before. He explains that a kiss is dveikus of spirit with spirit, as shown by Orpah, whose kiss was not genuine, and Ruth, who clung to Naomi because both had Jewish souls.

title.en: Why Shir Hashirim belongs to Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav asks how Shir Hashirim is Shlomo's when the Midrashim say it was sung at the sea and at Matan Torah, and compares Tehillim, which contains psalms said before Dovid. He answers that each Jew's neshamah has its own portion in Torah, as in the Midrash where Moshe heard Hashem say a halachah of the parah adumah in the name of Rabbi Eliezer; so Shir Hashirim belongs to Shlomo's neshamah even when said earlier.

title.en: Better than the wine of seventy nations

summary.en: The Rav explains 'ki tovim dodecha miyayin': yayin equals seventy, and Hashem's love is dearer to Klal Yisrael than everything the seventy nations offer when they urge the Jews to join them and escape the persecutions of galus. He ends with the death by a kiss, as with Moshe, when the soul leaves the body in the pleasure of dveikus with Hashem.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains 'Yishakeini mineshikos pihu' as the bond with Hashem through learning Torah, which is also the Jewish people's true weapon, and reads 'L'reiach shemanecha' as the fragrance of Hashem's miracles above nature that even the nations must sense.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to 'Yishakeini mineshikos pihu': the Torah is G-dliness itself, so one who learns is truly bound to Hashem, and he ought to feel its great sweetness, as the Ohr HaChaim writes and as Dovid HaMelech says. The kiss is the Shechinah speaking through a Jew's mouth in Torah and tefillah. With the Midrash he explains that the Oral Torah, renewed below and sent upward, is dearer than the Written Torah; that 'neshikah' means hashakah, a joining like two mikva'os; and that it means 'neshek', weapons. The Torah is the Jews' weapon: the miraculous survival of Jews in Eretz Yisrael comes only through those who learn, and Shlomo HaMelech's sixty warriors were sixty masechtos. Rashi reads the song as Klal Yisrael in exile remembering Sinai. On 'L'reiach shemanecha' he explains shemen as eight, above nature, connects it to Chanukah and Shavuos, and shows how Hashem's miracles spread like poured oil, so the nations hate Israel out of jealousy and some come to convert.

en: Because the Torah is G-dliness itself, a Jew who learns is truly joined to Hashem, and the Torah should be tasted as the greatest sweetness.
The 'kisses of His mouth' are the Oral Torah, which the Midrash calls dearer than the Written Torah because it is renewed on earth and goes up to Heaven.
'Neshikah' also means hashakah, contact like that of two mikva'os, so through Torah a Jew becomes one with Hashem.
'Neshikah' also means 'neshek', weapons: the Torah is the Jewish people's ammunition, and their survival in Eretz Yisrael is only in its merit.
Shemen is related to shemoneh, eight, the level above nature, which is why miracles, Chanukah and the giving of the Torah are bound to eight.
Hashem's miracles for Israel spread like the fragrance of poured oil, so the nations must acknowledge them, and they hate the Jews out of jealousy.

title.en: Torah as a kiss: bond and sweetness

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah is G-dliness itself, so learning bonds a Jew to Hashem, and he should feel its great sweetness, as the Ohr HaChaim and Dovid HaMelech say. The kiss is the Shechinah speaking through a Jew's mouth in Torah and tefillah.

title.en: Oral Torah, and hashakah like a mikveh

summary.en: From the Midrash the Rav explains that the 'kisses' are the Oral Torah, dearer than the Written Torah because it is renewed below and rises to Heaven, and that neshikah means hashakah, as water joined to a mikveh becomes part of it. Through Torah a Jew becomes one with Hashem, though in our generation few feel that sweetness.

title.en: Torah as the Jews' weapon in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Midrash reads neshikah as 'neshek', weapons. The Rav describes the hidden miracle of Jews living among hostile Arabs, recalls that the nations did nothing in the Holocaust and how Rommel was stopped, and concludes that the true army defending Israel is those who learn Torah.

title.en: Shlomo's sixty warriors and Rashi's reading

summary.en: The Rav asks how Shlomo HaMelech's sixty sword-bearing warriors fit with his having had no sword, and answers with the Midrash that they are sixty masechtos: Torah is the Jews' weapon. He then brings Rashi, who reads the song as Klal Yisrael in exile recalling Hashem's closeness at Sinai and awaiting its return with Moshiach.

title.en: 'L'reiach shemanecha': fragrance of poured oil

summary.en: On the third pasuk, the Rav explains 'shemen turak' as precious oil whose fragrance is sensed only when it is poured from vessel to vessel, and brings Rashi: Hashem's name spread through the miracles in Egypt, and the 'alamos' are the nations, some of whom loved Him and converted.

title.en: Seven and eight: nature and above nature

summary.en: The Rav contrasts yayin, seventy, the nations rooted in the seven days of creation, with shemen, from shemoneh, the eighth level above nature on which Hashem leads Israel. He shows this in the counting toward Shavuos, the Chanukah miracle of oil burning eight days, the eighth pasuk of Tehillim 19 about Torah, and the third month in both halves of the year.

title.en: Miracles today and why the nations hate Israel

summary.en: The Rav says the Torah is eternal, so the miracles of Krias Yam Suf are seen today too, and their fragrance forces the nations to acknowledge them. He explains that the nations hate even assimilated Jews because they know Israel is the chosen people, citing the Meshech Chochmah on Germany, and that some gentiles have the courage to convert.

catalogTitle: קיום המצות במחשבה דיבור ומעשה. אע"פ שהתורה לבוש לנשמה היא יותר גדול ממנה. התורה נשתלשל למטה עד שיש באפשריות של המוח גשמי להשיג אלקות.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the garments of Torah and mitzvos are greater than the soul they clothe, and how Hashem reduced His infinite will and wisdom into Torah so that a human mind can grasp it.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews the Tanya's teaching that a Jew fulfils the mitzvos in thought, speech and action, and that these become garments for the soul. He shows how thought enters a mitzvah, especially where the Torah gives its reason, as with tzitzis, which include all 613 mitzvos, and sukkah. An ordinary garment is secondary to its wearer, yet here the garment is greater, because Torah is G-dliness itself. He qualifies this: the soul in the body is only its lowest part, as he explains through yibum and chalitzah, and at its root the Jewish soul is even above Torah. Since the Creator and His wisdom are one, the human mind cannot grasp Him; it is a different category, as one cannot hear a picture. Out of kindness Hashem reduced the Torah into concepts of this world, like water turned to ice, wrapped like radium in lead, and like Shlomo HaMelech's chain of meshalim.

en: Thought, speech and action in Torah and mitzvos are garments for the soul.
Unlike an ordinary garment, which is secondary to its wearer, the garment of Torah and mitzvos is greater than the soul, because Torah is G-dliness.
The part of the soul inside the body is only its lowest part; at its root the Jewish soul is above Torah.
The human mind was made to understand this world and cannot grasp Hashem, not for lack of intelligence but because G-dliness is outside its category.
Hashem reduced the Torah into concepts of this world, such as the laws of damages, so that our minds can grasp it.
Where one finds Hashem's greatness, that He cannot be grasped, one finds His humility, that He lowered His will and wisdom into the 613 mitzvos.

title.en: Three garments: thought, speech and action

summary.en: The Rav reviews that a Jew fulfils the mitzvos in thought, speech and action, which become garments for the soul, and notes that a suit is secondary to the person who wears it. He shows how learning Torah and putting on tefillin involve all three, and how, where the Torah gives a mitzvah's reason, that reason becomes part of the mitzvah.

title.en: Tzitzis, sukkah and the reason in mind

summary.en: The Rav explains that tzitzis, which include all 613 mitzvos, differ from every other garment, and that the reason for sukkah is given in the Torah, so one keeps the reason in mind; where no reason is given, knowing one does a mitzvah is enough. He sums up thought, the brachah and the act, and asks how the garment can be greater than the soul.

title.en: Torah is G-dliness, so the garment is greater

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem and His wisdom are one, so Torah and every mitzvah are G-dliness itself, and the garment is more important than the soul. He notes that at its root the soul is higher than Torah, but sets that aside to speak of the soul as it is here.

title.en: The soul in the body and its root

summary.en: Through yibum and chalitzah the Rav explains that the soul within the body is only its lowest part, like the foot inside a shoe, while the rest reaches heaven as an encompassing light. He then explains that Yisrael preceded the Torah in thought and the world was created for them, so at its root the soul is above Torah, and the Tanya speaks of the soul as it is in the body.

title.en: Hashem reduced Torah into worldly concepts

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya that these garments are endlessly greater than the soul, and brings the Rambam that Hashem is the knower and the knowledge in one. Since our minds were made for this world, Hashem in great kindness reduced Torah into worldly cases such as an ox goring a cow.

title.en: Two meshalim: the picture and the water

summary.en: With a mashal he heard from his rebbe, seeing a symphony or hearing a picture, the Rav shows that the mind cannot grasp G-dliness because it is the wrong faculty, not a weaker one. He then compares how steam becomes water and ice, the same substance in coarser forms, to how Hashem lowered the Torah into a form our minds can hold.

title.en: No probing His greatness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem is called Ein Sof and that His greatness has no 'cheker', explaining the word as deep probing and philosophy, which cannot reach Him. In a partly garbled stretch he describes a person paying a high price for something a neighbor values at a quarter, and says the soul senses something special even when the mind does not.

title.en: His will and wisdom in the halachos

summary.en: The Rav reads that no thought can grasp Hashem's will and wisdom, which are the halachos of the Torah: that one who damages pays, and that one shelters in a sukkah though an architect would not advise it. He brings several pesukim and Chazal's teaching that where Hashem's greatness is found His humility is found, and reads the Tanya that Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the 613 mitzvos so the soul can grasp and fulfil them.

title.en: Radium in lead and Shlomo's meshalim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's greatness is that we cannot grasp Him and His humility is that He bent down to us, comparing Torah to radium carried safely in a lead container. He explains Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim as a chain, each explaining the one above it, as Hashem brought Torah down through the worlds to earth, so that people grasp it better than the angels.

oneLiner.en: On the pasuk 'your oils have a good fragrance', the Rav explains that Hashem's miracles and all holiness are hidden like silent oil, yet the final redemption will come with open wonders, and the memory of past miracles keeps Jewish love of Hashem alive even in times of concealment.

abstract.en: Continuing Shir Hashirim 1:3, the Rav teaches that miracles and holiness are hidden: the Mishkan's beams were covered, and Elisha's staff failed because Gechazi publicized the miracle. Only rarely, as in a story of the Sanzer Rav in Oberland, does a tzaddik reveal a wonder to sanctify Hashem's name. From the Midrash on oil, which pours silently and does not mix, he turns to the Jewish people, who may not mix with the nations; the return under Nechemiah came without miracles because of foreign wives. He weighs the Rambam's Moshiach, who needs no miracles, against the Raavad's, and argues the Rambam's is greater, since moving every Jewish heart is the greatest wonder. With the Yismach Moshe he shows that a promise made with Hashem's Name cannot be lost, explains why Chanukah lights stand below ten tefachim, and closes that remembered miracles keep emunah alive in hester panim.

en: Hashem's miracles, like all holiness and good deeds, are normally hidden, and an open miracle is the exception, used only to sanctify Hashem's name.
The Jewish people, like oil, do not mix with others, and the return for the Second Beis Hamikdash lacked miracles because many had married foreign wives.
The Rambam's Moshiach, who is known by his deeds rather than by miracles, is the greater Moshiach, since the greatest miracle is to bring Hashem into a Jewish heart.
A promise Hashem makes with the Shem Havayah stands above time and cannot be cancelled by sin, so the final redemption will come with miracles and wonders.
Jews keep loving Hashem even in times of hester panim because they remember the miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim, Chanukah and Purim.

candidateTopics: Moshiach in the Rambam and the Raavad
Second Beis Hamikdash and foreign wives
Hashem's promise with the Shem Havayah

title.en: Miracles are hidden, like a fragrance

summary.en: The Rav returns to the third pasuk of Shir Hashirim, 'your oils have a good fragrance', and explains that Hashem's miracles, like all holiness, are hidden and only their fragrance comes out. He brings the gold-covered beams of the Mishkan, which Rashi explains as tznius, and Elisha's staff, which failed because Gechazi talked about the miracle on the way.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav in Oberland

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Sanzer Rav came to a wedding in Oberland, a non-Chassidic region of Hungary, and revealed the hidden origin of the chasan, a wonder he showed because there they did not know there is a Ribono shel Olam. He then restates the rule: such openness is the exception, the open miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim were so the world would know Hashem, and holiness is always in tznius.

title.en: Oil that is silent and does not mix

summary.en: From the Midrash the Rav explains that poured oil makes no sound, and that oil does not mix: a drop of water in a full glass of oil pushes out a drop of oil, as a word of foolishness pushes out a drop of Torah. He applies this to the Jewish people, who may not mix with the nations, and shows that the return for the Second Beis Hamikdash came without miracles because of foreign wives, whom the people sent away at Nechemiah's word, contrasting this with today's assimilation.

title.en: The Rambam's Moshiach and the Raavad's

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that Moshiach need not show miracles and is recognized by his deeds, and the Raavad who disputes this and expects great wonders. He argues that the Rambam's Moshiach is the greater one, since the greatest miracle is to bring Hashem into a Jewish heart, and that so great a Moshiach is needed for a people sunk in the fiftieth gate of impurity.

title.en: Gathering the exiles with one word

summary.en: Illustrating the Rambam's sign of gathering the exiles, the Rav pictures Moshiach calling out on 47th Street and everyone leaving their shops open to follow him. He compares this to Moshe Rabbeinu's sign 'pakod pakadti', whose power was that the words entered Jewish hearts, and brings the tradition that at Moshiach's shofar even the worst meshumad will run after him.

title.en: Where the Beis Hamikdash will stand

summary.en: The Rav points out that the place of the mizbe'ach must be exact, yet today nobody knows it, and every group would bring its own view; Moshiach will say one word and all will accept it. Recalling Nechemiah again, he concludes that although the Rambam makes miracles no requirement, the plain meaning of the pesukim and Midrashim is that there will be great miracles.

title.en: A promise made with Hashem's Name

summary.en: The Rav asks whether our generation, worse than that of the Second Beis Hamikdash, will merit miracles. He brings the Gemara that Israel deserved miracles in Ezra's days but sin caused, the pasuk 'ad ya'avor amcha Hashem', and the Yismach Moshe's answer that a promise made with the Shem Havayah is above time and cannot be cancelled, and the final redemption is promised that way.

title.en: Chanukah lights below ten tefachim

summary.en: The Rav explains that although the Shechinah never descends below ten tefachim, the Chanukah light is lit below ten, in the public domain, at night, on the left side and in the darkest season, all places where the forces of impurity rule. The seforim say it kindles the light of Moshiach, who will come down to the lowest Jews and lift them up.

title.en: Loving Hashem in times of concealment

summary.en: Returning to the pasuk, the Rav says the Chanukah miracle came through oil, which does not mix, to purify Klal Yisrael, and reads 'alamos' as from 'he'elem', concealment: Jews love Hashem even in hester panim, as after the destruction in Europe. Their emunah holds because they remember the miracles of Yetzias Mitzrayim, Chanukah and Purim, whose fragrance still remains.

oneLiner.en: On the pesukim 'al ken alamos ahevucha' and 'moshcheini acharecha', the Rav explains how Klal Yisroel loves Hashem with self-sacrifice and youthful zeal, and how even in galus Hashem brings them into His inner chambers and they rejoice with Him.

abstract.en: The Rav learns Shir Hashirim 1:3-4. He first reads 'alamos' as 'al mos', unto death: throughout galus Jews gave their lives for Hashem, from the war against the Hellenists at Chanukah to the battle against the Communists in Russia and, in his day, against Reform and Conservative, at a time with no single leader for Klal Yisroel. A second reading is youthfulness: serving Hashem with zerizus, unlike the lazy man of Mishlei; he urges bochurim to use their years of youth, to keep growing in yiras shamayim, and to check the motive behind every kulah. A third reading has 'alamos' as the nations: souls from Sinai born among goyim smell the 'fragrance' of the miracles and convert. On 'moshcheini acharecha' and 'hevi'ani hamelech chadarav', he explains, with Rashi and the Midrash, that even in galus Hashem reveals new depths of Torah, as with Rabbi Akiva and Yechezkel, that His glory is in every shul, and he closes with the Midrash of the couple who took each other along.

en: 'Al ken alamos ahevucha' is read as 'al mos': throughout galus Jews loved Hashem to the point of giving their lives for Him.
In today's galus the main war is fought by Jews against Jews who abandoned the Torah, and the absence of a single leader of Klal Yisroel is one of the signs of ikvesa d'meshicha.
'Alamos' also means youthfulness: serving Hashem with energy and zerizus, and the years of youth are worth far more than later years.
Every kulah needs checking: one must ask whether it comes from the truth or from a leaning of the yetzer hara, and only a real danger, not a remote fear, excuses one from serving Hashem.
Some gentiles have Jewish souls from Sinai; they feel a drive toward Hashem, sense His miracles like a spreading fragrance, and come to convert, while the other nations remain indifferent.
Even in galus Hashem brings Klal Yisroel into His chambers: new depths of Torah were revealed in galus, through Rabbi Akiva, Yechezkel's vision in Bavel and the Talmud Bavli.
Hashem's glory is in every shul; one who does not see it must believe it, and treat the shul, a mikdash me'at, with awe.

title.en: 'Alamos': loving Hashem unto death

summary.en: The Rav reads 'al ken alamos ahevucha' together with 'ki alecha horagnu kol hayom' and explains that Jews gave their lives for Hashem throughout galus. His example is Chanukah, when Hellenized Jews tried to force Greek culture on Klal Yisroel and Matisyahu's few fought the many.

title.en: Today's war: Jews against Jews

summary.en: The Rav says that from Russia onward the main war against Torah Jews has come from Jews: the Communists, and now Reform and Conservative in Eretz Yisroel. He laments that there is no single leader of Klal Yisroel as in his youth, calls this a sign of ikvesa d'meshicha, and says one must cling to Yiddishkeit and to the true gedolim.

title.en: 'Alamos': youthful zeal in avodas Hashem

summary.en: A second reading from the Midrash: Jews love Hashem with youthfulness, full of energy and zerizus. The Rav brings the tefillah in Berachos, the opening of Shulchan Aruch and Shlomo HaMelech's field of the lazy man, then tells bochurim that the years of youth are the key to their lives and that one must keep growing in yiras shamayim or slip back.

title.en: Checking every kulah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mesilas Yesharim that every kulah needs checking and explains that one must ask whether a leniency comes from the truth or from a leaning toward the yetzer hara. With the lazy man who says there is a lion on the road, he distinguishes a real danger from a remote fear, which must not keep one from davening.

title.en: 'Alamos': the nations and the gerim

summary.en: A third reading: 'alamos' are the nations. The Rav explains that some gentiles carry Jewish souls that stood at Sinai; they find no rest until they come back to their root, and the fragrance of Hashem's miracles draws them, like Rachav, Rus and Yisro. The other nations stay passive and say Hashem no longer cares for the Jews, but Jews in galus hold on to Him with emunah and bitachon.

title.en: 'Moshcheini acharecha' and remembering the old love

summary.en: The Rav learns Shir Hashirim 1:4 with Rashi: Klal Yisroel asks Hashem to draw it after Him, recalls how He brought them into His chambers, and even in galus, as a 'living widow', rejoices in remembering His love, like a kallah who remembers her chassan's gifts. He brings the love of following Hashem in the desert and the Clouds of Glory, the reason for Sukkos.

title.en: Hashem's inner chambers in galus

summary.en: With the Midrash that Klal Yisroel's faults come from its neighbors, the Rav explains that in galus Hashem brought Jews into His inner chambers: Rabbi Akiva was shown what was not revealed to Moshe, Yechezkel in Bavel saw the Merkavah and that the Shechinah had come with the Jews, and the Talmud Bavli and the secrets of Torah were revealed in galus out of Hashem's compassion.

title.en: Emunah: Hashem's glory in every shul

summary.en: The Rav says that one who does not feel the sweetness of Torah and avodah must have emunah. He brings the Midrash 'who came into the beis haknesses and did not see My glory', and the seforim that 'nifteichu hashamayim va'ereh mar'os Elokim' spells emunah: one who does not see must believe. He speaks of awe in shul, a mikdash me'at, and of thanking Hashem for being let in.

title.en: The couple who took each other along

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash of a childless couple about to divorce; the husband let his wife take the most precious thing in the house, she took him, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai blessed them with children. He adds a teshuvah of the Chiddushei HaRim on such a case and a report he heard that the Sanzer Rav gave such a brachah, and applies 'nagila v'nismecha bach': in galus Klal Yisroel takes Hashem along.

oneLiner.en: On the words 'we will rejoice in You', the Rav explains that a Jew's joy on Yom Tov is in Hashem Himself, that the Jewish people live through the Yomim Tovim, and that the Chanukah lights bring the Shechinah and the light of Moshiach down to the lowest souls.

abstract.en: The Rav continues with Shir Hashirim, 'we will rejoice in You, we will recall Your love more than wine'. A person with strong emunah sees Hashem's hand in every salvation, and an upright Jew rejoices more in the closeness to Hashem than in the salvation itself. Through the Midrash, Shlomo's 'in You' explains Dovid's 'in it' in Hallel: the joy is in Hashem, not the day. Each Yom Tov carries its own light, best felt by learning its halachos, which warm a Jew more than wine. Citing the Rambam on the calendar, he shows that Klal Yisrael exists through the moadim. Purim and Chanukah are weekday festivals that give a boost in galus. Chanukah lights, lit below ten tefachim, on the left, in the public domain, in the darkest season, bring the Shechinah to fallen souls, as the story of the Chozeh of Lublin and an informer shows.

en: An upright Jew rejoices less in the salvation itself than in the closeness to Hashem that he felt through it.
The joy of Yom Tov is in Hashem, not in the day; the nations' holidays are empty eating and drinking.
Learning the halachos of each Yom Tov before it lets a Jew feel its light, and they warm him more than wine.
The Jewish people exist through the moadim; without them they would have died out spiritually.
On Chanukah the Shechinah comes down below ten tefachim to the most extinguished souls, and the light of Moshiach is revealed in the lights.

title.en: Rejoicing in Hashem, not in the salvation or the day

summary.en: The Rav returns to the verse 'we will rejoice in You': one with strong emunah sees Hashem's hand openly in every salvation, and an upright Jew rejoices most in the closeness to Hashem it showed him. From the Midrash he shows that Shlomo's 'in You' explains the 'in it' of Hallel, and contrasts the empty holidays of the nations with a Jew who feels kedushah on Yom Tov.

title.en: The light of each Yom Tov and its halachos

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Moshe told the moadim of Hashem' as Moshe conveying the message and light of each Yom Tov, which one feels by learning its halachos, before Chanukah the sugya in Gemara Shabbos. These halachos are the 'love' dearer than wine, and each Yom Tov leaves a message for the whole year.

title.en: The calendar and Jews in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that since semichah ended, the moadim depend on the calendar of Hillel and on Jews living in Eretz Yisrael. He explains the nineteen-year cycle and the tekufos of Shmuel and Rav Adda, and says Hashem always kept Jews in Eretz Yisrael because Klal Yisrael cannot exist without the moadim.

title.en: Purim and Chanukah: weekday festivals

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Purim and Chanukah, given in galus, are weekday festivals, to sustain Jews in a weekday state. Shabbos is like an oasis for a parched traveler in the desert, while Chanukah and Purim are like a boost for a car whose battery died on the road.

title.en: Shabbos keeps the Jews; joy without limit

summary.en: The Rav says the Zionists' national identity did not stop the nations' hatred; Jews remain Jews through Shabbos and Yom Tov. He contrasts the nations' songs of wine and the hangover after their holiday with a Jew who sings of Hashem, and explains 'they will be sated and delight': spiritual pleasure has no limit.

title.en: Unfit oils: souls lit on Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav brings a teaching of tzaddikim on the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah: they are souls too extinguished to be lit on Shabbos. On Chanukah, the one time the Shechinah comes below ten tefachim, even such souls can be kindled.

title.en: Lights in the domain of darkness

summary.en: The Rav explains that kedushah is oneness, the reshus hayachid, while the other side is division, the reshus harabim. The Chanukah lights are lit in the public domain, on the left, at night, in the darkest season of the year, when the nations hold their festival. He compares them to a doctor's house call: the Shechinah comes down to visit Jews in the weekday state of galus.

title.en: The light of Moshiach and the informer's candles

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the light of Moshiach is revealed in the Chanukah lights, and tells the story of the Chozeh of Lublin, who would not curse an informer because he saw his soul shine while he lit Chanukah lights. He ends with the two aspects of Moshiach in the parshiyos read at Chanukah time, where kedushah comes down below ten.

catalogTitle: התורה יורדת בסתר המדריגות כדי שכל אחד יוכל לתפוס בה' ועי"ז זוכה ליחוד נפלא ועצום בהקב"ה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on Tanya chapter four, that the Torah came down through hidden rungs so that every Jew can grasp it, and that through learning Torah and doing mitzvos a person is bound to Hashem Himself in a union greater than the souls in Gan Eden enjoy.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the idea that this world is an imaginary world, while the truth is that Hashem is present here as before creation. Since no thought can grasp Hashem and the Torah is one with Him, Hashem brought the Torah down like water, rung by rung, clothing it in halachos, words and physical mitzvos, as radium is held in a lead case. Thought, speech and even the shaking of a Jew in learning are clothed in Torah, so the whole person becomes a chariot for the Shechinah. We do not feel it because aveiros insulate the body from the soul, yet one should believe it. This is why one hour of Torah and mitzvos in this world is better than all of Olam Haba, where souls only enjoy the rays of the Shechinah. He compares it to embracing a king through his garments, digresses on the seven notes of creation and Shabbos, contrasts philosophers with ovdei Hashem through the Satmar Rav at his Shabbos table, and answers a question about water as chesed.

en: This world is an imaginary world in which Hashem hides Himself, while in truth He is present here just as before creation.
Since no thought can grasp Hashem and the Torah is one with Him, Hashem lowered the Torah through hidden rungs, like water flowing down, into halachos and physical mitzvos.
The Torah changed only its form, not its essence, like water that becomes ice or steam and stays the same water.
When a person learns Torah with thought, speech and action, his whole being is bound to Hashem and becomes a chariot for the Shechinah, even if he does not feel it.
Aveiros insulate the body from the soul, so the body does not feel the Shechinah that the soul knows is resting upon it.
In Olam Haba the souls enjoy only the rays of the Shechinah, while in this world Hashem Himself is present in the Torah and mitzvos, which is why one hour here is better than all of Olam Haba.
Embracing Hashem through the Torah is like embracing a king through his garments: the king himself is in one's arms.

title.en: This world as an imaginary world

summary.en: The Rav recalls that Hashem lowered Himself into the Torah and its mitzvos so every soul can understand it, and explains that the physical world we think is real is the imaginary world, while Hashem fills it as before creation.

title.en: Torah descends like water through hidden rungs

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Torah is compared to water that flows down to the lowest place, brings the mashal of radium held in a lead case, and shows how the Torah clothed itself in halachos like those of sukkah, which are all names of Hashem, changing its form but not its essence, like water, ice and steam.

title.en: Thought, speech, action and the shaking of a Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah reaches down past thought into speech and the physical actions of learning, even the shaking over a Gemara, tells the account of two mixed-up children recognized by their shaking, and explains the shaking with the passuk that the soul of man is a candle of Hashem.

title.en: Bound to Hashem, but insulated by aveiros

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who learns Torah is bound from head to toe to Hashem and becomes a chariot for the Shechinah, as great tzaddikim visibly felt, and that we do not feel it because aveiros insulate the body from the soul; still, he says, one should believe it and act accordingly.

title.en: One hour in this world is better than Olam Haba

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk of the shield of Hashem's will that surrounds the tzaddik and the Mishnah in Pirkei Avos that one hour of teshuvah and good deeds in this world is better than all of Olam Haba, explaining that here Hashem's full presence rests on a person, while in Olam Haba only a light of the Shechinah reaches the souls.

title.en: The pleasure of grasping: Ziv HaShechinah

summary.en: The Rav compares the rays of the Shechinah to the rays of the sun, describes the pleasure of understanding a sugya or a scientific discovery, and explains that this is the pleasure tzaddikim have in Olam Haba as they rise from level to level, while no creature, not even the angels, can grasp Hashem Himself.

title.en: Embracing the King through His garments

summary.en: The Rav explains that understanding a mitzvah through a blatt Gemara is grasping Hashem Himself, unlike the souls in Gan Eden, and answers that the physical clothing does not matter, with the mashal of embracing a king through garments and sleeves; he connects this to the passuk 'His right hand embraces me' and to the Torah given from the right, the attribute of chesed and water.

title.en: The seven voices: music, creation and Shabbos

summary.en: In a digression, the Rav explains that Kabbalas Shabbos begins with Mizmor l'Dovid Havu, whose seven voices are the seven notes of music with which the seven days were created, says this world is wonderful for one who uses it for closeness to Hashem, and describes the harmony of the third, the seventh day as the completion that lets us sing, and Eretz Yisrael and the Kinneres as the seventh of the lands and seas.

title.en: Tanya is for ovdei Hashem, not philosophers

summary.en: Returning to his point, the Rav explains that water is chesed and the source of every pleasure, so Hashem's right hand embraces a person through the Torah. He then says the Ba'al HaTanya wrote for ovdei Hashem: a philosopher may see depth in the Tanya but has no taste for the union with Hashem, like a person with no ear for music.

title.en: The Satmar Rav's Shabbos fish

summary.en: The Rav tells how he saw the Satmar Rav at his Friday night tish, his face flaming at Kiddush and eating the fish with delight because he felt the Shabbos in it, and tells of a poor Jew who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos for his challos and fish. He concludes that the Tanya spoke to Chassidim who understood and were delighted by it.

title.en: Why water is chesed: a question

summary.en: A listener asks that other sefarim describe water as passive and static; the Rav answers that this is a mashal, but in its depth water reaches out and spreads, and it goes down to lower places to bring growth to the world, unlike gas, which spreads but rises away.

oneLiner.en: On 'I am black but beautiful', the Rav explains that a Jew's sins are only an outer stain while his essence stays good, and that on Shabbos he returns to that essence and feels it.

abstract.en: The Rav explains Shir HaShirim 1:5-6: Klal Yisroel tells the nations that its blackness is only a sunburn, not its nature. Through the Midrash brought by Rashi, black in its own deeds but beautiful in the deeds of the Avos, he explains that a Jew is good in essence and his sins are incidental, which is why teshuvah helps him; he brings Malachi, that Hashem loves Yaakov and hates Esav even when their deeds look alike. A second Midrash reads the verse as black on weekdays and beautiful on Shabbos. The Rav describes Shabbos as the Jew's soul, digresses on Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch and reads his English essay on Shabbos, and then says a Jew must work all week to taste Shabbos, which is a day of love, a taste of Olam Haba and a return to the soul's source where sin does not reach. He ends with the Ba'al Shem Tov's custom of saying Hodu before Shabbos and with teshuvah on Erev Shabbos.

en: Klal Yisroel's blackness is like a sunburn: external and temporary, not its true nature.
A Jew is good in essence because he comes from the Avos; his sins are incidental, so teshuvah, a return to his roots, helps him.
Shabbos is the soul and life-spirit of a Jew; it is what makes him a Jew.
Hashem gave Shabbos as a gift and wanted the Jews to know what it is; a Jew must work during the week to feel its taste.
Shabbos is a day of love between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, a taste of Olam Haba, and a return to the place the soul was hewn from.
On Shabbos a Jew should feel like one freed from prison, sickness, the desert and the sea, which is why Hodu is said before Shabbos.

title.en: Black but beautiful: only a sunburn

summary.en: The Rav explains the verses: Klal Yisroel tells the nations, the 'daughters of Jerusalem', that it is black like the tents of Kedar but beautiful like the curtains of Shlomo, and that its blackness is only a sunburn. He adds that in the future Jerusalem will be the metropolis to which the other nations submit.

title.en: Good in essence, sinful only incidentally

summary.en: From the Midrash in Rashi, black in my deeds and beautiful in my fathers' deeds, the Rav explains that like begets like: a Jew coming from the Avos is good in essence, so teshuvah helps him, unlike a gentile. He brings Malachi, that Hashem loves Yaakov and hates Esav even when their deeds look alike.

title.en: Black on weekdays, beautiful on Shabbos

summary.en: A second Midrash reads the verse as black during the week and beautiful on Shabbos. The Rav compares Shabbos to an oasis after the desert, calls it the soul of the Jew, and brings the Midrash that Shabbos had no partner until Klal Yisroel was given to it.

title.en: Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch and the Haskalah

summary.en: Before reading Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch's essay on Shabbos, the Rav describes the destruction the Haskalah caused in Germany, how Rabbi Hirsch brought German Jews back, and why he wrote in German, ending with his answer to a maskil who criticized him for it.

title.en: Reading Rabbi Hirsch's essay on Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav reads in English from Rabbi Hirsch's essay: taking Shabbos from a Jew robs him of his richest jewel, and Shabbos, given to children, stays with them when all else fails. He comments that it is still pale, but a very good attempt to describe what Shabbos means to a Jew.

title.en: A gift from the treasury: tasting Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Hashem told Moshe He has a good gift in His treasury called Shabbos and to let the Jews know it, and Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin's word that one who keeps Shabbos without toiling for it will sit in Gan Eden like a block. He describes a Shabbos table of Torah and zemiros, and uses his own upset stomach, when good apple juice tasted bitter, to show why one must prepare all week.

title.en: Shabbos: day of love and return to the source

summary.en: Shabbos is the root of all pleasure and the source of Olam Haba; the Ramban explains there is no sin-offering on Shabbos because it is a day of love, which covers all sins. The Rav explains that the soul is hewn from the Kisei HaKavod and on Shabbos returns there, to the world of Klal Yisroel that sin does not reach, which ties the two Midrashim together.

title.en: Hodu before Shabbos and teshuvah on Erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains the Ba'al Shem Tov's institution of saying Hodu before Shabbos: the four who must thank Hashem are like a Jew leaving the prison, sickness, desert and stormy sea of the weekdays. He closes with the Gemara on checking one's garments on Erev Shabbos, read as checking one's betrayals, and with teshuvah and mikveh before Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that both burning chametz and immersing in a mikvah bring a person back to the root of creation, where all judgments are sweetened, and that a mikvah is an 'embassy' of the heavens made of fire and water.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by calling the reading of Shir Hashirim a preparation for Shabbos, a day of love, and says the same is true of immersing in a mikvah. Turning to the ten plagues, which struck Egypt and healed Israel, he asks why Rabbi Yehuda, who gave the plagues their simanim, also holds that chametz may only be destroyed by burning. Everything is built of four elements; removing one undoes the rest, but fire is the root of all four, and returning to the root uproots the evil and sweetens the judgments, as teshuvah does and as Noach's offering did. He ties this to the Haggadah, which draws down the salvations of the plagues. He then explains the mikvah: the heavenly mikvah is a river of fire, the earthly mikvah is its embassy, and a person who immerses, curled up and not breathing, is nullified and emerges reborn, with bitachon in Hashem.

en: Reading Shir Hashirim and immersing in a mikvah on Erev Shabbos are both preparations for Shabbos, a day of love.
Every thing is composed of the four elements, and removing one of them undoes the whole; but fire is the root of the other three.
Going back to the root of creation, before the sin, sweetens all judgments; this is the essence of teshuvah.
The Haggadah is not merely telling a story; it draws down the same lights and salvations that came at the Exodus.
The mikvah on earth is the 'embassy' of the heavens, which are made of fire and water, so one who immerses enters the heavens and the fiery river.
The core of the mikvah is bitul: one gives up breath and self like an unborn child and emerges a new person.

title.en: Shir Hashirim, mikvah and the ten plagues

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shir Hashirim is said as a preparation for Shabbos, a day of love, and that immersing in a mikvah on Erev Shabbos belongs to the same preparation; he announces he will speak about the mikvah. He then turns to the ten plagues as great revelations that struck Egypt and healed Israel.

title.en: Chametz and the four elements

summary.en: The Rav asks why Rabbi Yehuda, who gave the simanim of the plagues, is involved with how chametz is destroyed, and explains that chametz is the klipah. Since everything is made of the four elements, chametz can be undone through any one of them: crumbling into the wind, casting into water, or burning.

title.en: Sweetening judgment at its root

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rabbi Yehuda requires burning because the way to neutralize judgments is to go up to their root, where all is good. He brings a teaching of the Ba'al HaTanya: the same reason given for bringing the Flood is given for never bringing it again, because Noach's offering brought him back to the root of creation before the sin.

title.en: Teshuvah, the first Rosh Hashanah, Tishrei and Nissan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yerushalmi in which Wisdom, Torah and Hashem each answer what the sinner's punishment is, and explains that teshuvah goes back to the first Rosh Hashanah, before any sin. He contrasts the two beginnings of the world, Tishrei with the attribute of judgment and Nissan with mercy, and says that in Nissan burning the chametz nullifies the judgments and reaches the four letters of Hashem's Name, the root of the four elements.

title.en: Yehuda, fire and the Haggadah

summary.en: The Rav links the four elements to the four camps in the desert, with Yehuda at the head corresponding to fire, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda, of the soul of Yehuda, insists on burning to uproot evil at its root. He explains that the Haggadah draws down the salvations of the plagues, which is why the Tanna'im multiply the plagues, and that Rabbi Yehuda's simanim, initials that contain the whole word, reach deeper still.

title.en: The heavenly mikvah of fire

summary.en: The Rav explains that there is a mikvah in heaven made not of water but of fire, the fiery river formed from the sweat of the singing angels, in which souls and angels immerse. A kosher mikvah on earth contains that fire within its water; since the heavens are fire and water, the mikvah is the heavens' 'embassy', and one who immerses enters the heavens.

title.en: Immersing in the Name of Hashem

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the mikvah a person surrenders his breath and life and enters the heavens and the Name of Hashem, whose letters he describes as four by ten, like a reshus hayachid, giving the forty se'ah of a mikvah. He brings that the Ba'al Shem Tov would immerse when he needed a salvation, and the kavanah to curl up like an unborn child and emerge reborn.

title.en: Bitul, rebirth and bitachon

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man who tried to make 310 immersions by dipping a finger, and says the point of the mikvah is bitul, not counting. He brings the Rambam that purity comes on emerging, the Arizal's mikvah kavanos, and that mikvah and the word 'rachitz' both mean trust in Hashem; he closes with the Reishis Chochmah that one's soul immerses above when one immerses below.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the first luchos give the creation of the world as the reason for Shabbos while the second luchos give the Exodus: at Matan Torah every Jew was a prophet who saw the Creator in the world, and after the sin of the golden calf they needed the miracles of Egypt that they had seen with their own eyes.

abstract.en: The Rav opens a series on avodas Hashem by beginning with Shabbos, 'the first of the holy days', which Klal Yisroel was commanded at Marah even before Matan Torah. He contrasts the two versions of the Ten Commandments: in the first luchos Shabbos is 'zachor' and its reason is that Hashem made the world in six days; in the second luchos it is 'shamor' and the reason is the Exodus from Egypt, and Kiddush mentions both. He then describes at length the wonders and beauty of creation, from the seasons and fruits to the human body, and argues that heretics deny the Creator only because they do not want to be bound to Him, illustrating this with two stories and the Chovos HaLevavos's parable of the painting. The Exodus, witnessed by millions and handed down through the generations, could not be denied, and at Matan Torah every Jew became a prophet. That is the answer: prophets see the Creator in the world itself, but after the golden calf they lost that level, so the second luchos point to the Exodus, whose ten plagues mirror the ten utterances of creation in reverse.

en: Shabbos could not wait until Matan Torah: Klal Yisroel was already commanded about it at Marah, soon after leaving Egypt.
The first luchos give creation as the reason for Shabbos, the second luchos give the Exodus, and Kiddush mentions both.
The whole world, its seasons, fruits and creatures and the human body, is full of wonders that show a Creator.
Heretics know the truth deep down; they deny it only because admitting it would oblige them to obey Hashem.
The miracles of the Exodus, seen by millions and passed down from generation to generation, cannot be denied, and at Matan Torah every Jew became a prophet.
As prophets they saw the Creator in the world, so the first luchos speak of creation; after the golden calf they lost that level, so the second luchos speak of the Exodus they had witnessed.

title.en: Beginning with Shabbos, commanded at Marah

summary.en: The Rav opens a series of talks on avodas Hashem and begins with Shabbos, 'the first of the holy days'. He notes that he mostly repeats what is written in the holy sefarim, and that Shabbos was commanded at Marah, before Matan Torah, because it could not wait the forty-nine days.

title.en: Two luchos, two reasons for Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav reads the Shabbos commandment of the first luchos, 'zachor', whose reason is the six days of creation, and of the second luchos given after the sin, 'shamor', whose reason is the Exodus from Egypt. He notes that Kiddush on Friday night says both.

title.en: The wonders of creation and why heretics deny them

summary.en: The Rav describes the beauty of the world through the seasons, the fruits with their different colors and tastes, the human body and even a tiny fly, all showing the Creator. He says heretics refuse to admit it because they would have to obey, and tells of a woman who asked a newspaper to stop writing about the miracles of a war in Eretz Yisroel because they kept her from going to the beach on Shabbos.

title.en: The falling ceiling in Telz

summary.en: The Rav tells of a club of irreligious young men in Telz where one of them took his own life, after which the plaster of the ceiling below kept falling. Rav Bloch, the Rosh Yeshivah, answered from Shulchan Aruch that blood of the dead must be buried; once the soaked floorboards were buried the ceiling held, and one of the young men stopped coming to the club because he now saw there is a Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: The parable of the painting

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chovos HaLevavos's parable of a beautiful painting that someone claims came about when a wind spilled bottles of paint onto paper, and adds a house that built itself. Nobody would believe that, yet the heretic believes the far more wondrous world made itself, because he does not want to admit the truth he knows.

title.en: The Exodus and Matan Torah, seen by millions

summary.en: The Rav says there was one time when the truth had to be admitted: the Exodus, with the ten plagues that correspond to the ten utterances of creation and the splitting of the sea, seen by millions and handed down as history. At Matan Torah every Jew became a prophet and heard Hashem speak, and no other nation has such a tradition.

title.en: Why the reason changed after the golden calf

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: as prophets, like the Ba'al HaTanya who saw the Creator when he looked at the ceiling, the Jews at Matan Torah saw the Creator in the world, so the first luchos give creation as the reason for Shabbos. After the golden calf they lost that sight, so the second luchos point to the Exodus they had witnessed, whose ten plagues repeat the ten utterances of creation in reverse order.

catalogTitle: ע"י לימוד תורה - כביכול תופס ה' בתוכו' וה' מתיחד בו ביחוד עצום ונפלא.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Tanya chapter five: when a Jew truly understands Torah he and the Torah envelop each other, and since Hashem encased Himself in the Torah, this is a union with Hashem that no mitzvah and no angel reaches.

abstract.en: The Rav first reviews a passage of the Ba'al HaTanya about ten Jews: the Shechinah rests on any ten, so a group that sits idle 'squeezes' the Shechinah, and he brings the Maggid of Mezritch's saying that an angel would be burnt up among ten Jews. The Ba'al HaTanya therefore urges simple people to learn the aggados of Ein Yaakov, where the deepest secrets of the Torah are hidden. Turning to chapter five, the Rav explains that a mitzvah envelops a person only from outside, while Torah understood with the mind is a double union: the person grasps the subject and the subject envelops him. Though no thought can grasp Hashem, He encased Himself in the halachos like radioactive matter in lead, so a Jew who understands a halacha grasps Hashem's will. Therefore Torah is called food and mitzvos clothing. He ends with sukkah as surrounding light and the Torah of Simchas Torah as inner light.

en: Wherever ten Jews gather the Shechinah rests on them, so idle talk there presses on the Shechinah; the Rav says ten Jews together should learn Torah.
Many aggados of the Gemara that seem senseless hide the highest secrets of the Torah, which is why the Ba'al HaTanya tells simple people to learn Ein Yaakov.
A mitzvah envelops a person from outside, but Torah that is understood is a double union: the person envelops the Torah and the Torah envelops him.
No thought, not even of angels, can grasp Hashem, yet a Jew grasps Him in Torah, because Hashem and the Torah are one and He encased Himself in the halachos.
The mitzvah of knowing Torah with the mind surpasses even the mitzvah of speaking words of Torah, because the Torah enters within the person.
Torah is therefore called food, which becomes part of the body, while the mitzvos are called clothing.

title.en: The Shechinah among ten Jews

summary.en: The Rav reviews the Ba'al HaTanya's words that the Shechinah rests wherever ten Jews gather, and brings the Maggid of Mezritch's saying that an angel would be burnt up among them. When they sit idle, he explains, they squeeze the Shechinah, which is one cause of the length of the golus.

title.en: The hidden secrets in the aggados

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Ba'al HaTanya tells the common people to learn Ein Yaakov: aggados that sound like nonsense, such as the bird whose egg destroyed sixty cities, wrap the highest secrets of the Torah. Answering a listener who asks whether this is dangerous, he says that the straight walk in the Torah's ways while the crooked stumble.

title.en: Perek five: Torah envelops from both sides

summary.en: Opening chapter five, the Rav notes that the Tanya develops one theme step by step. A mitzvah envelops a person like a cloak, but Torah is more: one who is immersed in learning grasps the Torah within him while it surrounds him from without, a double union.

title.en: Grasping Hashem encased in Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that although no thought, not even an angel's, grasps Hashem, a Jew who learns does, because Hashem and the Torah are one. He compares it to radioactive matter held safely in a lead box and to a caress through a sleeve, and reads the Tanya's words on the mind enveloping the subject it understands.

title.en: A halachah is Hashem's will

summary.en: Unlike a mathematical equation, a halachah is Hashem's wisdom and will, even in cases that may never happen, such as the Gemara's question about one born with two heads. Understanding it is a wondrous two-way union that has no parallel in the physical world.

title.en: Knowing Torah surpasses every mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mitzvah of knowing Torah is above all mitzvos, even above speaking words of Torah, since in lulav or tefillin the holiness only surrounds the person. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya's ruling about thinking Torah before the blessing, and shows with a boy learning 'tashma' that each person must work to his own full capacity.

title.en: Torah is food, mitzvos are clothing

summary.en: Torah that is learned becomes a person's food and the mitzvos he does become his clothing, which the Rav says is why clothing costs more than food: money should be spent on mitzvos, while Torah is given free. Like bread absorbed into the body, understood Torah becomes part of a person, and spoken Torah is both garment and food.

title.en: Sukkah surrounds, Torah is within

summary.en: After a question about kavanah in mitzvos, the Rav explains that the sukkah is a surrounding light and that on Simchas Torah the inner light of the Torah follows. He connects this to the generation of the flood, which merited only the ark, a kind of sukkah, and to Shavuos and Shemini Atzeres, which have no special mitzvah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that melachah is the product of the curse after Adam's sin while Shabbos is pure blessing, so Shabbos is kept not as a day of rest from labor but as a holy day whose kedushah enters even its simple foods.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by contrasting melachah with blessing. In Gan Eden bread and garments grew ready on the trees; only after the sin did bread and clothing require long chains of labor, and the thirty-nine melachos correspond to the curses given to Adam, Chavah, the earth and the serpent. Shabbos, which Hashem blessed, is therefore free of melachah, and lesser holy days allow correspondingly more work; in the future, when everything is blessing, every day will be Shabbos. The rest of Shabbos must be for Heaven's sake: Moshe won a weekly day off for the slaves in Egypt on practical grounds, but at Sinai Hashem commanded Shabbos as holiness. Through the Beis Aharon's three levels in Yismechu, stories of tzaddikim and their Shabbos food, and the Shabbos lights, the Rav shows that the kedushah of Shabbos enters its simple foods, and closes that oneg Shabbos is joy in that kedushah.

en: Melachah came into the world through the curse after Adam's sin; before it, bread and garments grew ready on the trees of Gan Eden.
Shabbos is a time of blessing, which is why no melachah is done on it; the more blessing a day holds, the less melachah it allows.
Resting on Shabbos must be for Heaven's sake, not in order to recover from the week's work.
The Jews kept a day of rest in Egypt as weary slaves, but the Torah commands Shabbos because it is a holy day through which Hashem sanctifies them.
The kedushah of Shabbos enters its lights and its foods, so that even simple Shabbos dishes have a heavenly taste.
Oneg Shabbos is joy with the kedushah of Shabbos, not merely enjoying more food.

title.en: Melachah as the opposite of blessing

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Gan Eden Adam needed no work, since bread and garments grew on the trees, and that Adam stayed in Gan Eden over Shabbos after the sin. After the curse, bread and clothing require long chains of melachos, and the thirty-nine melachos correspond to the curses received after the sin.

title.en: Shabbos is blessing, so no melachah

summary.en: The Rav explains that because Hashem blessed Shabbos it has no melachah, while Yom Tov, Chol Hamoed and Rosh Chodesh, with less kedushah, allow progressively more work. In the future everything will grow as blessing and it will be a day that is all Shabbos; meanwhile the rest of Shabbos must be for Heaven's sake, not for recovering from the week.

title.en: Moshe's day of rest in Egypt

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Moshe persuaded Pharaoh to give the exhausted Jews a weekly day off so they would work better, which he compares to the modern law of diminishing returns, and Moshe chose Shabbos. He then explains the pasuk 'Ach es Shabsosai tishmoru': no longer a slave's day off as in Egypt, but Shabbos kept as a holy day.

title.en: Three levels of keeping Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Beis Aharon on the three groups named in Yismechu: shomrei Shabbos who rest, korei oneg who make Shabbos a delight, and mekadshei shevi'i who make it holy, the level Hashem desires. He applies this to rising early to learn, leaving time to learn on Shabbos afternoon, and davening better on Shabbos.

title.en: Stories of the taste of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells of a poor chassid who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos for his challah, brings the Midrash about the gentile who asked a Tanna what gave his food its taste and was answered 'Shabbos', and tells the story of the cholent of Reb Yechezkel of Kuzmir, whose secret was that he put in a handful himself with the words 'l'kavod Shabbos'.

title.en: Shabbos lights and simple Shabbos foods

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos light and Shabbos food differ from those of the week, bringing the Midrash that Hashem blessed Shabbos with the light, and says the purer a Jew is from sin the more kedushah shines in them. The Shabbos dishes are simple, yet have a heavenly taste, and he tells how a chassid of Reb Aharon of Karlin said Nishmas while preparing the fish, and the Rebbe sensed Nishmas in it.

title.en: A Shabbosdik kugel, not a kugeldik Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav notes that Jews eat the same Shabbos foods in a set order because of the secrets in them, and explains the zemer Menuchah v'Simchah's line 'Nishmas kol chai… echol b'simchah' as eating the Nishmas that was said over the fish. He closes with a tzaddik's saying that some have a Shabbosdik kugel and others a kugeldik Shabbos: oneg Shabbos is joy with its kedushah, kept for Heaven's sake.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos is a gift Hashem sanctified from above, yet a Jew only feels its holiness when he prepares himself for it all week, like a clean cup for precious wine.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the difference in kiddush: on Yom Tov one says 'who sanctifies Israel and the seasons', on Shabbos only 'who sanctifies the Shabbos'. Shabbos was fixed and sanctified by Hashem at Creation, while Yom Tov depends on the Jews who sanctify the months and on how they prepare, as with removing chametz, which the Radvaz, following the Zohar, identifies with the yetzer hara, counting the Omer before Shavuos, and Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur before Sukkos. Shabbos, by contrast, is a gift from Hashem's treasury. Yet a precious gift needs a clean vessel: expensive wine poured into a dirty cup tastes of nothing. Through stories of tzaddikim and chassidim, the Gemara's account of the Amoraim preparing for Shabbos, and Shammai who ate all week in honor of Shabbos, the Rav teaches that the whole week, with teshuvah and mikvah before Shabbos, is the preparation that lets one feel Shabbos.

en: Shabbos was fixed and sanctified by Hashem, while the holiness of Yom Tov comes through the Jews, who sanctify the months and prepare for each festival.
Each Yom Tov has its own preparation: removing chametz, which stands for the yetzer hara, before Pesach; the Omer before Shavuos; Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur before Sukkos.
Shabbos is a gift from Hashem's treasury, but like precious wine it needs a clean vessel; one who comes to Shabbos unprepared does not taste it.
The preparation for Shabbos is the whole week: learning, davening, guarding the eyes, thoughts and mouth, beginning already on Motzaei Shabbos.
Even the great Amoraim stopped learning to prepare for Shabbos with their own hands, and Shammai ate all week in honor of Shabbos.
Before Shabbos one must do teshuvah and immerse in the mikvah, and the Rav adds that immersing on Shabbos morning is greater still.

title.en: Who sanctifies Shabbos and who Yom Tov

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Yom Tov kiddush says 'who sanctifies Israel and the seasons' while Shabbos says only 'who sanctifies the Shabbos'. He explains that Hashem fixed Shabbos at Creation, while the Jews fix Yom Tov through the months, and each festival is because of them; on a deeper level, holiness either comes down as Hashem's gift or is drawn by the Jews sanctifying themselves.

title.en: Yom Tov's holiness and preparing for Pesach

summary.en: Like a sofer who makes a Sefer Torah holy, the Jews make Yom Tov holy by preparing for it, while Hashem Himself blessed and sanctified Shabbos. The Rav applies this to Pesach: removing chametz, with a story of Rav Yisrael of Vizhnitz and his gabbai at bedikas chametz, and the Radvaz's answer, from the Zohar, that the stringency of chametz is because it is the yetzer hara.

title.en: Shavuos, Sukkos, and Shabbos as a gift

summary.en: The Rav describes the preparation of the Omer days, refining one's middos, before Shavuos, and of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and the four days before Sukkos. Shabbos is different: he brings 'see that Hashem gave you the Shabbos' and the Gemara that Shabbos is a good gift from Hashem's treasury, which one must make known so the Jews value it.

title.en: Fine wine in a dirty cup

summary.en: The Rav gives a mashal of a hundred-dollar bottle of wine poured into a cup left dirty with sour milk, which tastes of nothing because the vessel is soiled. A Jew who did teshuvah, went to the mikvah and sang 'Kah Echsof' before Shabbos receives the gift in a clean cup and feels the holiness of Shabbos.

title.en: Coming to Shabbos unprepared

summary.en: The Rav describes bochurim who spend Erev Shabbos playing ball and then have no taste in Shabbos, and tells of bochurim who came to him with this complaint, one of whom found taste after davening in Stolin. He brings the Zohar that 'Bereishis' spells 'yarei Shabbos', fear of Shabbos, and says one must make a cheshbon hanefesh and prepare all week, from Motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Every mitzvah toward an uplifted Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings from sefarim that every mitzvah and every daf of Gemara should be done with the intent to merit an uplifted Shabbos, and a segulah of tzaddikim to bless one another on Thursday night. Since Shabbos is a gift from a very high place, no one can prepare enough; he tells of a poor Karliner chassid who asked Hashem to give Shabbos to his wine and fish, and of the Satmar Rav whose face burned while eating fish on Shabbos.

title.en: Two storekeepers whose Shabbos burned

summary.en: The Rav tells of a young hidden tzaddik with a store, whose fiery kiddush puzzled his learned neighbor; he answered that while selling to the women he thought of Shabbos kiddush, while the neighbor at kiddush thought of the women he had watched. He then tells of Reb Nissan Pilchik in the Stoliner beis medrash, a peddler who blazed on Shabbos and, leaving a melaveh malkah at dawn, cheered another Jew that in six days it would be Shabbos.

title.en: How the Amoraim prepared; teshuvah and mikvah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Rav Safra, Rav Huna and Rava stopped their learning to prepare for Shabbos with their own hands, the daily song that counts the days toward Shabbos, and Shammai who ate all week in honor of Shabbos. He concludes that one must prepare with teshuvah and immersion before Shabbos, reading 'Lev tahor' as a hint to tevilah, and adds that immersing on Shabbos morning is greater still.

catalogTitle: כנגד עשר ספירות דקדושה יש זה לעומת זה “עשר כתרין דמסאבותא” . סימן להשראת הקדושה - שבטל להקב"ה ובטומאה להיפוך.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter six, the Rav explains that opposite the ten holy powers of the soul stand ten 'crowns of impurity', and that holiness rests only on what is batel to Hashem, which every Jew is in potential.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tanya chapter six: just as the soul of holiness has ten powers, the soul from kelipas nogah has ten powers of impurity, 'zeh l'umas zeh'. He notes that only impurity is called 'crowns', because it attributes greatness to itself, and links its ten to the ten sons of Haman. Impurity, he adds, is never truly ten but nine or eleven, shown by the Teivah's eleven amos, the Mishkan's eleven goat-hair curtains and the eleven spices of the ketores. He then explains that the middos can serve Hashem or nonsense; there is no neutral reshus, and pointless pursuits are 're'us ruach', a breaking of the soul's connection. Holiness rests only on what is batel to Hashem; every Jew is batel in potential, as the history of mesiras nefesh shows, an inheritance from Avraham Avinu. He closes with a story of the Ba'al Shem Tov's daughter and questions from listeners.

en: Opposite the ten holy powers of the soul there are ten powers of impurity from kelipas nogah, so a person can become a seat either for holiness or for impurity.
The powers of impurity are called 'crowns' because impurity has a sense of self and attributes greatness to itself.
The ten of impurity are not truly ten but nine or eleven; the number ten is reserved for holiness.
There is no neutral reshus: whatever is not done for the sake of Hashem belongs to the other side, the sitra achra.
Holiness rests only on what is batel to Hashem, and every Jew is batel to Hashem at least in potential.
The readiness of Jews to give their lives for Hashem is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu.
