nine and eleven in the realm of impurity
ketores and nullifying the sitra achra

title.en: Ten powers of holiness and ten of impurity

summary.en: The Rav recalls the ten holy powers of the soul and introduces Tanya chapter six: opposite them, 'zeh l'umas zeh', stand ten powers of impurity in the soul from kelipas nogah, so a person can become a seat for either side.

title.en: Why impurity is called 'crowns'

summary.en: The Rav points out that the word 'crowns' appears only for impurity, because impurity is haughty and sees itself as something. He lists the seven bad middos from the four elements and the intellect above them, and links the ten crowns to the ten sons of Haman in the Megillah.

title.en: Impurity is nine or eleven, never ten

summary.en: The Rav explains that the ten of impurity only appear to be ten and are really nine or eleven. He shows this from Rashi's eleven amos of the Teivah, the eleven goat-hair curtains of the Mishkan, the eleven spices of the ketores and the order in which they are listed, and the eleven verses said on Motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Middos for Hashem or for nonsense

summary.en: The Rav explains that the same middos can serve Hashem, such as chesed, gevurah for milchemes Hashem and pride in being a Jew, or can be spent on nonsense, like insisting on a designer tie or anger over trifles. There is no reshus: it is either a mitzvah or an aveirah, and the middos follow the level of a person's intellect, as with a child.

title.en: Re'us ruach: breaking the connection

summary.en: The Rav explains that worldly pursuits that are not for Hashem are 'havel' and 're'us ruach'. He illustrates with a ball game, where grown men scream over a stitched pigskin, and explains re'us as breaking: such pursuits sever the soul's connection to Hashem like a cut wire.

title.en: The ice cream: two sides of the fence

summary.en: The Rav explains 'sitra achra' as the other side of the fence. Ice cream eaten to lift one's spirits is a mitzvah, and recreation in measure for health is good, but indulgence for its own sake falls to the other side, since there is no reshus.

title.en: Holiness rests on what is batel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's holiness rests only on what is batel to Him: the angels in fact, like a machine run by its operator, and every Jew at least in potential, as shown by Jews throughout history who gave their lives rather than commit avodah zarah.

title.en: Chalav akum and readiness for mesiras nefesh

summary.en: Citing the Tzemach Tzedek on Jews who are not ready for mesiras nefesh, the Rav digresses to chalav akum: government-inspected milk, the views of Rav Moshe Feinstein and the Chazon Ish, and a story of a Rebbe who made himself vomit milk he learned was chalav akum. He returns to say such things can dull a person's readiness to give his life.

title.en: Avraham's inheritance and Fayvish the thief

summary.en: The Rav explains that readiness for mesiras nefesh is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, and that the Ba'al HaTanya says a Jew who sins remains holy because he is ready to die for Hashem. He tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov's daughter Adel, who said Hashem chose wisely, since even a thief named Fayvish gave his life rather than convert, and adds that at the shofar of Mashiach even the farthest Jew will run after him.

title.en: Questions: intention and Krias Shema

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Rav suggests that an act begun for Hashem keeps its first intention even if the mind wanders, as with learning Gemara, and that the morning declaration of readiness for mesiras nefesh carries through the day. On whether to imagine actual death at Krias Shema, he says the sefarim say to imagine it.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos is a gift that comes with its own path, erev Shabbos, and describes how a Jew prepares for it with honor, mikveh, teshuvah, shame and longing.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the outward honor of Shabbos: a white tablecloth, candles, silver vessels and Shabbos clothing, which leave a Shabbos grace in a Jewish home all week. The soul too needs clothing: the neshamah yeseirah must find a body made white through teshuvah, and so one goes to the mikveh on erev Shabbos with teshuvah. A kosher mikveh joins itself to rainwater from heaven, and so before Shabbos one connects to tzaddikim and their sefarim. He adds tevilah on Shabbos morning, before Nishmas, and tells how the Chida learned from the Rebbe Reb Elimelech that erev Shabbos is like Yom Kippur. From the Gemara that Shabbos is a gift and the halachah that a giver gives generously, including the path, he explains that erev Shabbos is the path to Shabbos, to be walked with Torah, teshuvah, shame and waiting, and he ends by urging the bachurim to attend the Friday night gatherings.

en: Honoring Shabbos with a white tablecloth, candles, silver and special clothing gives the Jewish home a Shabbos grace that remains all week.
The neshamah yeseirah must be received with a body made clean and white through teshuvah, which is why one goes to the mikveh on erev Shabbos with teshuvah.
Shabbos is a gift from Hashem, and one who gives a gift gives generously, including the path to it; erev Shabbos is that path.
Erev Shabbos is like Yom Kippur: one must do teshuvah, feel shame before the Ribono shel Olam for the week's failings, and enter Shabbos with that shame.
A Jew waits for Shabbos all week; 'shomer Shabbos' means one who waits for Shabbos.

candidateTopics: teshuvah and shame on erev Shabbos

title.en: The outward honor of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav describes how a Jew honors Shabbos by tidying the house, covering the table with a white cloth, lighting candles and using silver candlesticks and a silver cup, and changing into Shabbos clothes as the Gemara teaches. This leaves a Shabbos grace on the Jewish home even in the middle of the week.

title.en: Teshuvah and the mikveh before Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav says the neshamah yeseirah must find a body made white through teshuvah, so one goes to the mikveh on erev Shabbos with teshuvah and immerses at least three times. He explains that a mikveh is full of holy names in its halachos and must come from rainwater from heaven, and that ordinary water becomes kosher by joining it; so too before Shabbos one connects to tzaddikim and their sefarim.

title.en: Shabbos-morning tevilah and Nishmas

summary.en: The Rav says it is a great matter to immerse on Shabbos morning too, because a greater holiness comes down then, and the neshamah yeseirah of the morning comes at Nishmas. He brings the zemer Tzama Nafshi of Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra, which longs for Nishmas, and says one can have in mind in the mikveh to merit a proper Nishmas.

title.en: Erev Shabbos as Yom Kippur: the Chida and the Rebbe Reb Elimelech

summary.en: The Rav brings from Ohr LaShamayim that erev Shabbos is like Yom Kippur and needs teshuvah. He tells how the Chida asked the Rebbe Reb Elimelech in heaven why his name caused a greater stir there, and the Rebbe Reb Elimelech answered that in his kitchen on erev Shabbos the women would ask one another forgiveness as on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Shabbos is a gift that includes the path

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk that Hashem 'gave' Shabbos and the Gemara that Shabbos is a good gift from His treasury. Citing the Chiddushei HaRim, he explains the halachah that a buyer of a pit must buy access to it while a recipient of a gift gets the path too, since a giver gives generously; so Hashem gave also the path to Shabbos, erev Shabbos, as seen from the double portion of manna on Friday.

title.en: Friday as a holy day of preparation

summary.en: The Rav says Friday is a holy day, criticizes bachurim who spend Friday playing ball, and says one prepares with a blatt Gemara, the mikveh and a chassidish sefer. He connects the sixth day and the sixth year to blessing, says Friday corresponds to Yosef HaTzaddik and holiness, and calls for teshuvah and shame before Hashem on erev Shabbos.

title.en: Shame, remembering and waiting for Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings that the word Bereishis holds 'yarei boshes' and that one enters Shabbos with shame. He says a Jew remembers and longs for Shabbos all week, from Motzei Shabbos on, cites the Rambam that one should prepare early on Friday and then sit and wait for Shabbos as for a great guest, and says each mitzvah of the week can be done with Shabbos in mind.

title.en: Shomer Shabbos, and the Friday night gatherings

summary.en: The Rav explains 'shomer' as waiting, as with Yosef's dreams, so a shomer Shabbos is one who waits for Shabbos. He then stresses the Friday night and Shalosh Seudos gatherings with zemiros and talk of tzaddikim, urges the bachurim not to miss them, recalls the taste such a gathering left in him as a young man, and closes with Gut Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos is received by preparing for it all week and by being together with other Jews, and that Shabbos completes the 'seven notes' of creation, so that on Shabbos the day itself sings and a Jew must sing along with it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the teaching of the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov that a Jew longs for Shabbos all week, bringing Shammai, who ate all week in honor of Shabbos, and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'lo seva'aru esh': light the fire at the start of the week. He then explains that Shabbos is received by being together with Jews: holiness is unity, and when Jews gather only their good combines, like small candles forming one great flame. Shabbos was meant to last forever before Adam's sin, so 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' speaks of the future day that is entirely Shabbos. Music has seven notes like the seven days; only with Shabbos is the 'piano' complete, which is why Kabbalas Shabbos sings Psalm 29 as its seventh chapter. On Shabbos the day itself sings, so Jews sing along: in davening, at the seudos and above all at shalosh seudos, whose real seudah is the singing.

en: A Jew prepares all week for Shabbos, through learning, davening and good deeds, so that he becomes a vessel for its holiness.
Holiness is unity and impurity is division; when Jews come together on Shabbos their good joins into one great good, while their faults do not combine.
Before Adam's sin the world was to be one endless Shabbos, and 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' speaks of that future day that is entirely Shabbos.
Music has seven notes because the world was created in seven days, each with its own note; with Shabbos, the seventh, the scale is complete and one can sing.
On weekdays the Levi'im sang the song of the day, but on Shabbos the day itself sings, so Jews must sing along with Shabbos in harmony.
The real seudah of shalosh seudos is the singing, eaten together with other Jews in the beis medrash.

title.en: Waiting for Shabbos all week

summary.en: The Rav brings the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov that a Jew longs for Shabbos all week, the Gemara about Shammai who ate all week in honor of Shabbos, and the Chasam Sofer's reading of 'lo seva'aru esh' as a call to kindle the fire from the start of the week.

title.en: Shabbos together with other Jews

summary.en: The Rav explains that a great way to receive Shabbos is to be together with Jews, citing Rav Yisroel of Vizhnitz. Each Jew has his own good; holiness is unity and evil is division, so when Jews gather their good joins like many small candles into one flame, while their faults do not.

title.en: Adam's endless Shabbos and the psalm of the future

summary.en: The Rav explains that Adam was placed in Gan Eden for a Shabbos that should never have ended, but the sin ended it; 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos' therefore sings of the future day that is entirely Shabbos. He adds that on Friday night one praises Hashem more than all week, with the six chapters of Kabbalas Shabbos.

title.en: Seven notes and the seven days

summary.en: The Rav explains that music has seven notes because each day of creation has its own note, corresponding to the seven middos, with Shabbos as malchus. Only with the seventh is the 'piano' complete, which is why after the six chapters of Kabbalas Shabbos comes Psalm 29 with its seven 'kol Hashem', and then Lecha Dodi can be sung.

title.en: On Shabbos the day itself sings

summary.en: The Rav brings the song the Levi'im sang each day in the Beis Hamikdash and explains that on weekdays they sang, but on Shabbos the day itself sings. Therefore Jews must sing along with Shabbos in harmony, in davening, on Friday night and at shalosh seudos; this is the idea of zemiros.

title.en: Who really steers the world

summary.en: Going through Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos, the Rav explains that the foolish do not see that the wicked flourish only to be destroyed, for Hashem runs the world. He tells of Rav Aharon Kotler and the car with a second steering wheel for a child, and explains 'tzaddik katamar yifrach' with the date palm and the cedar.

title.en: Zemiros, shalosh seudos and singing together

summary.en: The Rav explains that with the full seven notes Jews sing zemiros on Shabbos, together, above all at shalosh seudos in the beis medrash, where 'da hi seudasa' is said after eating and before singing because the singing is the real seudah. He closes with his shul's practice of giving the best seats near the chazzan to the bochurim so they sing and daven with fire together, like the malachim who give each other permission.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos, the seventh, is the day on which all of creation completes its song, and that Jews sing along with Shabbos in their zemiros and at seudos made holy by the presence of the Avos and of Shabbos itself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer: Hashem made seven days, seven lands and seven seas, and in each the seventh is the chosen one: Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael and the Kinneres. Music too has seven notes, and the Levi'im spent five years learning its wisdom. The Kinneres, the seventh sea, is named for the kinor, the harp, and is shaped like one; when the seven are complete the song begins. Through a story of the Stoliner patting the Blazhever Rav on the shoulder, he explains the passuk that the border 'touches the shoulder of Yam Kinneres'. Of all the Levi'im's daily psalms only Shabbos's is called 'a song', because Shabbos itself sings and Jews sing along with it. He speaks of the power of a niggun, of achdus in singing together, of preparing all week to feel Shabbos, of the holiness of Shabbos food, and of a Shabbos table where Shabbos itself is invited.

en: In each set of seven the seventh is the chosen one: Shabbos among days, Eretz Yisrael among lands, the Kinneres among seas.
The Kinneres is named for the kinor, a harp: once seven are complete, the song can begin.
Only the Levi'im's psalm for Shabbos opens with 'mizmor shir', because Shabbos itself sings, and Jews join its song.
The essence of a niggun is the unity of its notes, and Shabbos is the day of achdus, so Jews singing together at the table and at shalosh seudos is a great pleasure to Hashem.
A person who did not prepare and guard himself during the week cannot feel the taste of Shabbos.
Shabbos food is holy, and a Shabbos meal must invite the 'King', Shabbos itself, through divrei Torah, zemiros and holy conversation instead of weekday talk.

title.en: The seventh sea: why the Kinneres sings

summary.en: The Rav brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer on seven days, lands and seas, ties them to the seven notes of music that the Levi'im studied, and asks about the passuk on the border at Yam Kinneres. He explains that the Kinneres, the seventh sea, is named for the harp and shaped like one, and that Eretz Yisrael sings.

title.en: The Stoliner's pat on the shoulder

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Stoliner, after hearing the Blazhever Rav's holy kriyas haTorah, patted him on the shoulder so that he would daven Musaf. From this he explains the passuk: on Shabbos the border goes around Eretz Yisrael and pats the singing Kinneres on its shoulder.

title.en: Only Shabbos's psalm is a song

summary.en: The Rav lists the psalms the Levi'im sang each day and notes that only Shabbos's opens with 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos'. Shabbos itself sings, and since no person would dare sing to Hashem on his own, Jews sing along with Shabbos.

title.en: A day of song, and the power of a niggun

summary.en: The Rav brings the Apter Rav that Shabbos is the time of singing, and a saying that one would sooner believe the seven seas dried up than that a Jew who can sing does not sing on Shabbos. He describes the singing of Friday night, the day meal and shalosh seudos, and explains that composing a true niggun takes a spirit close to ruach hakodesh.

title.en: Niggun as unity, Shabbos as achdus

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the niggunim of tzaddikim and of new composers sent down from Heaven, contrasting a real melody with a cat walking on a piano. The essence of a niggun is the unity of its notes; Shabbos is the secret of 'echad', so Jews singing zemiros together is a great pleasure to Hashem, and he laments those who leave before the zemiros.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and preparing for Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav mentions Yedid Nefesh and calls shalosh seudos the peak of Shabbos's achdus, as in 'Atah echad'. He explains that one who did not guard himself in holiness during the week cannot feel Shabbos, urges preparing from motzaei Shabbos, and contrasts those who daven Shabbos with sweetness with those who talk during davening.

title.en: The Avos at the seudos; holy Shabbos food

summary.en: The Rav says the Avos come to the Shabbos seudos of Jews united in achdus, and that Shabbos food contains holiness. He tells how Reb Dovid'l Biderman of Yerushalayim ate a spoiled cholent in Meron, saying one may not disgrace Shabbos food.

title.en: Inviting the King to the Shabbos table

summary.en: The Rav says the day itself is the oneg, and brings a mashal of a man who prepared a feast for the king but never invited him. So a lavish Shabbos meal without calling in Shabbos is lacking; the table should hold divrei Torah, zemiros and stories of tzaddikim, not business talk.

catalogTitle: הטומאה הוא כקוף בפני אדם. החילוק בין קדושה וטומאה - ביטול להקב"ה. יניקת הקליפה מבחינת אחוריים' שלש קליפות הטמאות וקליפת נוגה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 6, the Rav explains that tumah imitates kedusha like a monkey imitates a man, that the whole difference is bittul to Hashem, and that the klipos live only from a tiny spark drawn from the 'back side' of holiness.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the idea that tumah mimics kedusha: the kuf imitates the hei as a monkey imitates a man, and Achashverosh's feast imitated the Beis HaMikdash. The difference is bittul: kedusha is nullified to Hashem, while tumah stands as an independent entity. He shows how Torah learned with yiras Shamayim and every gathering of ten Yidden draw the Shechinah, even the ten spies. A separate entity lives only from a tiny spark of kedusha given 'from behind', renewed every moment, and that spark is in exile; the Yid's task is to free it, and Chanukah and Purim bring kedusha down to the lowest places. He then distinguishes the three impure klipos, which cannot be elevated now, from what is nourished through them, explains the four klipos and the chayos of Yechezkel's Merkava, and closes with male and female in kedusha and in the sitra achra, the seven nations as middos, and why the inanimate is not listed.

en: Tumah has ten sefiros like kedusha and imitates it, like a monkey imitating a man, but it is not batel to Hashem.
Torah learned with yiras Shamayim makes a person batel and brings the Shechinah, while ten Yidden together always have the Shechinah with them.
A separate entity gets its existence through countless contractions, from the 'back side' of kedusha, and this is renewed at every moment.
The spark of kedusha that gives life to tumah is in exile, and the task of a Yid is to extract and redeem such sparks.
What draws its life from the three impure klipos cannot be elevated in this world, until Mashiach comes.
In kedusha the male, chesed, rules over the female, din, while in the sitra achra the female is stronger.

title.en: Tumah imitates kedusha like a monkey

summary.en: The Rav explains that tumah mimics kedusha: the kuf imitates the hei of Hashem's Name, and Achashverosh's feast imitated the Beis HaMikdash. The difference is that kedusha is batel to Hashem while tumah stands on its own, cut off from its supply; yet every Yid is inwardly batel.

title.en: Torah with yiras Shamayim and the ten

summary.en: The Rav explains why the Shechinah rests on one who learns Torah, provided he learns with yiras Shamayim, comparing Torah without it to an empty capsule or an unplugged radio. He then shows that ten Yidden always have the Shechinah, and that even the ten spies, from whom davar shebikdusha is learned, had it because inwardly they were tzaddikim.

title.en: Life from the back side, renewed each moment

summary.en: The Rav explains that whatever is not batel is a separate entity, yet it exists only through Hashem's word, contracted countless times into a tiny spark given from the 'back side'. He stresses that creation is not a historical fact but happens anew every moment.

title.en: The spark in exile and Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tanya's chiddush that even the energy of a rasha doing an aveirah is created at that moment from Hashem, a tiny spark that is in exile. He connects this to Chanukah, when the Shechinah comes below ten tefachim, and says the avodah of a Yid is to redeem such sparks.

title.en: A world mostly evil; Shabbos and Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav explains that this world is the world of klipos, mostly evil, as seen in nature. On Shabbos and Yom Tov a Yid rises above it, since melachah is a curse; on Chanukah and Purim, days when work is permitted, kedusha comes down to him. He ties this to Eliezer leaving the curse for blessing and to Shabbos Mevarchim Kislev.

title.en: Three impure klipos and the Merkava

summary.en: The Rav explains that the lower level of klipos, the three impure klipos, cannot be elevated until Mashiach. He brings the four klipos Yechezkel passed on the way to the Merkava, explains why the Ba'al HaTanya does not spell them all out, and shows from the lion and eagle of the Merkava how gevurah becomes impure on its way down. An audience question on mentioning resha'im follows.

title.en: What draws life from the impure klipos

summary.en: The Rav goes through the levels of creation, domem, tzome'ach, chai and medaber, and explains that the existence of non-kosher animals and of forbidden growths like orlah and kilai hakerem comes from the three impure klipos, which is why they are forbidden from their inception. He notes that the Tanya does not list domem and begins to explain why.

title.en: Chesed over din: male and female

summary.en: The Rav explains that in kedusha the male, chesed, is meant to dominate the female, din, and digresses to criticize the modern equality movement, contrasting it with the harmony of Jewish homes. He connects this to Esav's wives going first and to giving the right side precedence over the left.

title.en: The Or HaChaim's dream and the seven nations

summary.en: The Rav brings the Or HaChaim's dream of a male and a female dog, showing that in the sitra achra the female is stronger. He maps the seven nations onto the middos, explains that the Girgashi is malchus and left voluntarily, which is why domem is batel and not listed, and sums up the perek: ten crowns of tumah exist mainly in this world, while kedusha is batel to Hashem.

oneLiner.en: The Rav describes how people who strive higher keep Shabbos: guarding their speech, davening and learning at length, and reaching the peak of Shabbos at shalosh seudos with the zemer Bnei Heichala.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with speech on Shabbos: the kedushah of Shabbos limits a person's words to zemiros, brachos and Torah, and he should avoid talk that has no connection to Shabbos. He ties the three Shabbos meals to the Avos, with Friday night the meal of Yitzchak, and calls melave malka the meal of Dovid HaMelech. He discusses tefillas chatzos, a takanah and not an obligation, and tells of Rebbe Elimelech's melave malka. Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested on Shabbos, a higher person keeps Shabbos with his speech too, while still making the Shabbos table pleasant for his family. He then speaks of the long Shabbos davening, Torah learned on Shabbos, Shabbos as a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and the great ratzon of Shabbos afternoon. He closes with shalosh seudos: little eating, the Arizal's zemer Bnei Heichala sung with dveikus, the angels who come to look, and the forces of evil that cannot enter.

en: The kedushah of Shabbos limits speech: words of zemiros, brachos and Torah, and not talk that has no connection to Shabbos.
The Friday night meal is the meal of Yitzchak, the three Shabbos meals correspond to the Avos, and melave malka is the meal of Dovid HaMelech.
Because Hashem created the world with speech and rested on Shabbos, a higher person keeps Shabbos with his speech as well.
The Shabbos davening is longer, with many mizmorim not said during the week, and Torah learned on Shabbos is far higher than Torah learned during the week.
The high point of Shabbos is the afternoon, a time of great ratzon and rachamim.
At shalosh seudos one eats very little; its essence is the zemiros, above all Bnei Heichala, sung together with dveikus.

title.en: Speech on Shabbos and the Shabbos meals

summary.en: The Rav explains that the kedushah of Shabbos limits speech to zemiros, brachos and words of holiness, and warns against talk unconnected to Shabbos. He ties the Friday night meal to Yitzchak, the three meals to the Avos, and melave malka to Dovid HaMelech.

title.en: Tefillas chatzos and Rebbe Elimelech's melave malka

summary.en: The Rav explains that tefillas chatzos is a takanah and not an obligation, since a great level cannot be made a duty, and calls it the tefillah of Dovid. He then tells how Rebbe Elimelech kept melave malka with only tea and instructed his children about it.

title.en: Higher people keep Shabbos with their speech

summary.en: The Rav explains that since the world was created with speech and Hashem rested on Shabbos, higher people refrain from idle words on Shabbos, yet must make a pleasant Shabbos table for their family. He brings the halachic side of not speaking about weekday work, the story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mother, and a reading of 'bechorish uvakatzir tishbos' as silence.

title.en: Tefillah and Torah on Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Divrei Emes that tefillah is the essence of Shabbos and describes the longer Shabbos davening with mizmorim not said during the week. He speaks of resting well so as to daven properly, of a fixed time for a chassidishe sefer, and of Torah learned on Shabbos being far higher than weekday Torah.

title.en: 'Between Me and Bnei Yisroel' and Shabbos afternoon

summary.en: The Rav compares Shabbos to the private talk of two close friends, a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel. For the choshuve Yidden Shabbos is a yichud with Hashem, and its high point is the afternoon, a time of great ratzon unlike weekday mincha; he speaks of eating shalosh seudos together with a minyan.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and the Arizal's zemiros

summary.en: The Rav explains that at shalosh seudos one hardly eats and the essence is the zemiros, above all Bnei Heichala sung together with dveikus. He says the Arizal composed a zemer for each of the three meals, explains 'Bnei Heichala' as the King's palace children invited to eat with Him, and mentions the kabbalistic names of the meals, which he says he cannot explain.

title.en: Longing, angels and the closed door to evil

summary.en: The Rav describes the longing of shalosh seudos and how every small bite of the meal is precious. Angels come to see Jews sitting at shalosh seudos, the harsh judgments of weekday mincha are absent, and, as the zemer says, the brazen forces of evil cannot enter.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why shalosh seudos is the 'will of all wills', a time beyond time and without boundaries, and moves from there to Shabbos as a source of forgiveness and to the power of kiddush.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to the three seudos of Shabbos and focuses on shalosh seudos. It is called raava d'raavin, the will of wills: all of Shabbos is a time of favor, and from mincha on comes a still greater et ratzon. A Jew should then awaken a strong desire to become upright, and even one who feels nothing gains by sitting with friends in love. Time and place are created things; before creation Hashem had a will to create, and shalosh seudos, before the first Sunday, stands above time. He demands seriousness at the table and tells of the Rebbe of Rimanov who once pushed a man for chatting then. Shalosh seudos, a boundless inheritance of Yaakov, extends past the end of Shabbos. He then speaks of Shabbos atoning for sin, the need to learn its halachos, the angels' blessing, teshuvah before kiddush, and the Satmar Rav's kiddush.

en: Shalosh seudos is called raava d'raavin because all of Shabbos is a time of favor, and from mincha a still greater et ratzon begins, a will within the will.
At shalosh seudos a Jew should arouse a great desire to become upright from now on, and if he cannot, he should at least want to have that desire.
Shalosh seudos stands above time: it corresponds to the moment before creation when Hashem willed to create the world, so it is a time to will to be created anew as an upright Jew.
Shalosh seudos is a boundless inheritance like Yaakov's, so its holiness continues for those still sitting at it after the time of Shabbos has passed.
Shabbos kept properly brings forgiveness of sins, but one cannot be a shomer Shabbos without learning the halachos of Shabbos.
Kiddush is testimony that Hashem created the world, so the Bnei Yissaschar says to do teshuvah before kiddush, and it must be said or heard with great kavanah.

title.en: Shalosh seudos as raava d'raavin

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the three seudos correspond to the tefillos of Shabbos, says that shalosh seudos is a time for words of Torah and not idle talk, and explains why it is called the will of wills. He says a Jew should then resolve to become upright, or at least want to want it.

title.en: When one feels nothing: sitting with friends

summary.en: The Rav compares a Shabbos without feeling to Avraham at the Akeidah, who saw the place from afar yet served with acceptance of the yoke. He explains that sitting at shalosh seudos with friends in love, like the angels who receive from one another, lets even one without enthusiasm absorb it, as standing near a tzaddik helps in davening.

title.en: Shalosh seudos is above time

summary.en: The Rav explains that time and place are created things, bringing the Gemara that the aron took up no space. Before creation there was no time, only Hashem's will to create; shalosh seudos, before the world's first day, is that time above time, so a Jew can then will to be created anew, and it is a great time for yeshuos, especially with a minyan.

title.en: Seriousness at shalosh seudos; the Rimanov story

summary.en: The Rav asks that people sit seriously and not chat while waiting for shalosh seudos, using the minutes for Tehillim or a sefer. He tells of the Rebbe of Rimanov, who never bothered a Jew except once, when he pushed a man chatting at shalosh seudos, because it is a holy time.

title.en: Shalosh seudos extends Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the name 'shalosh seudos' means it includes all three meals, and that its et ratzon lasts past bentching and even past the time, so for those still sitting it is still Shabbos. This benefits souls released from Gehinnom on Shabbos; he notes two views in the seforim on how this works.

title.en: Torah after the time; Yaakov's boundless inheritance

summary.en: The Rav says tzaddikim teach that divrei Torah at shalosh seudos should be said after the time, when the et ratzon is greater. He explains that Avraham and Yitzchak were promised Eretz Yisrael with borders, but Yaakov was promised that he would spread out in every direction, a nachalah without boundaries; shalosh seudos is Yaakov's inheritance, so the clock cannot end it.

title.en: Shabbos, forgiveness and teshuvah before kiddush

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one who keeps Shabbos properly is forgiven even for idolatry, and stresses that being a shomer Shabbos requires learning its halachos, at least in Kitzur Shulchan Aruch before Mishnah Berurah. He brings the Gemara of the two angels who bless one who says Vayechulu, the dispute of the Maharal and the Taz whether teshuvah is needed, and the Bnei Yissaschar that one should do teshuvah before kiddush, since kiddush is testimony and a rasha cannot testify.

title.en: Kiddush with kavanah; the Satmar Rav's kiddush

summary.en: The Rav tells children to say or follow kiddush in a siddur with great kavanah, and describes hearing the Satmar Rav's kiddush, when the whole beis medrash seemed to testify to creation, and the gathering of tzaddikim in Williamsburg after the war. He ends with a tzaddik who told people needing a yeshuah to come before kiddush, since one who says Vayechulu becomes a partner in creation, and closes the series on Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why the first parsha of tefillin speaks only of a 'remembrance' while the later ones speak of 'totafos', and shows how a bar mitzvah is a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim in which the boy adds to the beauty of Hashem's own tefillin.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by linking the bar mitzvah with tefillin, then notes that the parsha of Kadesh calls tefillin a 'remembrance between your eyes', while the other parshiyos say 'totafos'. He gives two answers. The first parsha speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn, so it is only a remembrance, as Chazal explain 'zichron teruah' of a Rosh Hashanah on Shabbos. And, from the Imrei Emes, in the desert the Jews had only the first two parshiyos, while 'totafos' means four. He explains tefillin as attachment to Hashem and the bar mitzvah as a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim, tells of Reb Dovid'l of Tolna leaving his boyhood games, and teaches that the boy must know his worth as Hashem's firstborn, add to the beauty of Hashem's tefillin, and search himself by the light of Torah as he enters his fourteenth year. He closes with a brachah.

en: The first parsha of tefillin calls them only a 'remembrance' because it speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn.
Following the Imrei Emes, in the desert the Jews wore tefillin with only the first two parshiyos, so the first parsha could not yet say 'totafos', which means four parshiyos.
Tefillin express a Jew's attachment to Hashem, and a bar mitzvah is a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim, leaving childish, yetzer-hara things for the service of Hashem.
A bar mitzvah boy must know how precious he is to Hashem, as Hashem's firstborn.
Hashem's tefillin speak of the beauty of the Jewish people, and the bar mitzvah boy must add to that beauty.
Entering his fourteenth year, the boy must search himself by the light of Torah for any 'chametz' that needs to be cleared out.

title.en: Bar mitzvah as a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav explains tefillin as attachment to Hashem and the bar mitzvah as leaving childish things for the service of Hashem, tells how Reb Dovid'l of Tolna took leave of his boyhood play at his bar mitzvah, and from the parsha of Kadesh li chol bechor teaches that the boy must know he is precious to Hashem.

title.en: Adding to Hashem's tefillin; the fourteenth year

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's tefillin speak of the beauty of the Jewish people and that the boy must add to it, applies 'Or l'arba'ah asar bodkin es hachametz' to entering the fourteenth year, calls the first year after bar mitzvah the firstborn of a whole life, and closes with a brachah for the boy, his family and the final redemption.

catalogTitle: ביאור קליפת נוגה - “קדושים תהיו” - כנגד פריעה. (ישמעאל ומצוות מילה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains klipas nogah, the middle layer that a Jew can elevate by using permitted things l'shem shamayim, and shows the same pattern in milah and priyah, which he connects to Yishmael's claim on Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav contrasts the three wholly impure klipos, which can never be elevated, with klipas nogah, a scale that tips toward kedushah or tumah depending on intent. Kosher food is nogah: eaten l'shem shamayim it rises like a korban, eaten in excess it sinks. Citing the Ramban on 'kedoshim tihyu' and a psychologist's view that enjoyment is a real human need, he sets two conditions: no excess, and l'shem shamayim. Reading Tanya chapter seven, he explains that nogah is all good above but mixed below, and that meat and wine taken for an expanded mind for Torah, or for oneg Shabbos, are elevated. He finds the same rule in milah, where three layers are cut off and the fourth, priyah, is pulled up. This leads to Yishmael's 'empty' milah, Chevron as the place of milah, Shechem as the place of priyah, and the Shaagas Aryeh's chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are not obligated in priyah.

en: The three impure klipos can never be elevated, while klipas nogah is like a scale that tips toward kedushah or tumah depending on how it is used.
Kosher food eaten l'shem shamayim rises like a korban; eaten without need it is drawn into tumah until teshuvah lifts it.
Enjoyment is a real human need, but it must not be in excess and must be for the sake of serving Hashem.
Nogah is entirely good above but mixed with bad in this world; using it for good separates the good and raises it.
In milah the three layers cut off correspond to the three impure klipos, and priyah, the fourth layer pulled upward, corresponds to klipas nogah.
Bnei Yishmael, whose body stems from the three impure klipos, can repair only through milah and have no share in priyah, which corresponds to nogah.

title.en: Two extremes and the middle of klipas nogah

summary.en: The Rav reviews the previous chapters: through mitzvos a person becomes a seat for kedushah, through aveiros a seat for the three wholly impure klipos. He introduces klipas nogah as a middle layer, like a scale that can tip either way, unlike forbidden food, which can never be elevated.

title.en: Kosher food tips up or down; the Ramban on kedoshim tihyu

summary.en: Kosher food, bound up with the body, is klipas nogah: eaten l'shem shamayim it rises like a korban, eaten without need it is drawn into tumah until teshuvah lifts it again, while the harm of forbidden food stays even after teshuvah. He brings the Ramban on 'kedoshim tihyu' that even permitted pleasures must be sanctified, or a person becomes a degenerate with the Torah's license.

title.en: Why a person needs enjoyment, and its limits

summary.en: The Rav relates a psychologist's point that a person fed without tasting would break down, so enjoyment is a real need; but it must not be in excess and must be l'shem shamayim. A cookie to perk up one's learning is fine, a cookie because of a pleasant aroma is excess, and he cites his rebbe Rav Mendlowitz on a Midrash about the Leviasan's belly being in America.

title.en: Tanya ch. 7: the vital soul and permitted things

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of chapter seven: the vital soul of a Jew, the life of kosher animals, birds and fish, permitted produce, and permitted deeds and words draw from klipas nogah, not from the three impure klipos. He illustrates with someone talking about a ball game, which is no aveirah, and explains that nogah in its source above, the brightness around Hashem in Yechezkel, is entirely good.

title.en: Elevating nogah: meat, wine and oneg Shabbos

summary.en: In this world nogah is a mixture of good and bad on the borderline between the impure klipos and kedushah; used for good, the good separates and rises. He brings the example of fat meat and fragrant wine taken to gain an expanded mind for Torah, citing Rava, and distinguishes this preparation for a mitzvah from oneg Shabbos and Yom Tov, which is a mitzvah in itself.

title.en: Milah and priyah; Yishmael's empty milah

summary.en: The Rav shows the same rule in milah: the three layers cut off correspond to the three impure klipos, while the thin fourth layer of priyah is pulled up and elevated, like klipas nogah, and similarly the fourth year of a newly planted tree. He turns to Bnei Yishmael, circumcised at thirteen, and the Zohar that Eretz Yisrael was given to them for their empty milah and stays barren in their hands; the Gemara calls its renewed fruitfulness the clearest sign of the geulah.

title.en: Every place in Eretz Yisrael is a halachah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Temurah about the halachos forgotten after Moshe Rabbeinu's passing, which Osniel ben Kenaz restored through his pilpul, and an explanation that every place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah. Kiryas Sefer held those halachos, so mastering them let Osniel conquer the place; the plain meaning and the drash are both true.

title.en: Chevron, the place of milah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chevron is the territory of the mitzvah of milah, Avraham Avinu's own mitzvah, which is why he bought the Me'aras HaMachpelah with money. The Arabs, who claim Eretz Yisrael through their milah, fight hardest over Chevron, but he says Hashem will shake them out of the land like a sheet, since their milah is only an imitation.

title.en: The imitation and the genuine son of Avraham

summary.en: Responding to a listener, the Rav brings the Ba'al HaTurim on the passage of Yishmael's end followed by the offspring of Yitzchak ben Avraham: Yishmael claims to be the son of Avraham, while Yitzchak is the genuine one. He says each generation has a rasha who embodies Yishmael's accusation, in his time Arafat, whose name he shows equals 'Yishmael ben Avraham' in gematria.

title.en: Shaagas Aryeh: milah without priyah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shaagas Aryeh's chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are obligated only in milah, not priyah, and confirms it from Kabbalah: their body stems from the three impure klipos, so they cannot repair nogah. He adds a gematria on 'tachlis', a Midrash he heard from Rav Mendlowitz, and the halachah that a gentile may bring only an olah, not a shelamim, since only a Jew can make eating into avodah.

title.en: Shechem, the place of priyah, and the closing

summary.en: The Rav explains that priyah was given in Yehoshua's time, and Yehoshua comes from Yosef, whose purchased portion is Shechem, so Shechem is the place of priyah as Chevron is the place of milah. He closes that the work of klipas nogah is harnessing bodily pleasure to Hashem's will, like fourth-year fruit, and ends with a story of a seminary professor who spent his whole hour on the root of one word.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a bris in the week of Parshas Ki Savo, the sixth week of consolation and the week of the middah of yesod, is a good sign, since the avodah of that week, like the bris, is to remove the orlah and reveal the good hidden in every Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the verse calling the curses of Ki Savo 'the words of the covenant', and explains that the tochachah's harsh words are vessels of blessing that must be uncovered. That uncovering is bris milah: every Jew has good in him, and his avodah, beginning with the bris, is to remove the orlah covering it. Ki Savo is the sixth of the seven weeks of consolation, the week of yesod, the middah of the bris, and its avodah is to reveal that good. So too is Elul's avodah, hinted in the verse about the circumcision of the heart whose initials spell Elul. The haftorah's words about the nations he compares to milah and periah, and it ends with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim'. A bris in this week is therefore a good sign, and he blesses the child, the family and Klal Yisrael.

en: The Rav says the curses of Ki Savo, called 'the words of the covenant', are in truth vessels of blessing that need to be uncovered.
Every Jew has good in him, and his avodah, beginning with bris milah, is to remove the orlah that covers it.
Parshas Ki Savo is the sixth of the seven weeks of consolation, corresponding to the middah of bris, yesod, and its avodah is to reveal the good.
The avodah of Elul is the circumcision of the heart, as hinted in the verse whose initials spell Elul.
A bris in the sixth week, the week of 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', is a good sign that the child will be a tzaddik.

He compares the haftorah to milah and periah, calls a bris in this week a good sign, and closes with brachos.

catalogTitle: בר מצוה: bar mitzva Chaya Surah

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Jewish kiddushin is learned from the purchase of Me'aras HaMachpelah: a Jewish marriage is a bond of souls that outlives the body, and a bar mitzvah, when a boy receives his soul and the Torah as his kallah, is a wedding of the same kind.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Me'aras HaMachpelah, through which, the Midrashim say, Jewish prayers and souls pass. The Gemara learns that a woman is betrothed with money from Avraham's purchase of the cave from Efron. He asks why the happiest moment of life should be learned from a grave, and answers that Avraham wanted his bond with Sarah to continue beyond life: a Jewish marriage is a union of souls that existed before birth and outlasts the body. He then brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is like a wedding: the boy receives his soul, and the Torah, given as a kallah and an inheritance of all Jews, becomes his. Through the Chasam Sofer on Haman he shows that the Torah lives in every Jew. Finally he contrasts Efron's dust with the fire of zrizus the Torah needs, and blesses the boy, noting that the holy ancestors attend the simcha.

en: The Rav says, citing the Midrashim, that Jewish prayers and souls pass through Me'aras HaMachpelah on their way up.
Kiddushin with money is learned from Avraham's purchase of the cave, because a Jewish marriage is a bond of souls that continues even after death.
A couple's souls were joined even before they were born, so every Jewish marriage is a union of souls.
A bar mitzvah is like a wedding: the boy receives his soul, which is Torah, and the Torah becomes betrothed to him as a kallah.
The Torah is the inheritance of every Jew and lies in his inner self even if he is not a talmid chacham.
Torah must be served with zrizus, the fire that rises, in contrast to the dust of Efron that brings sadness.

title.en: Kiddushin learned from the Machpelah

summary.en: The Rav describes Me'aras HaMachpelah as the gate of prayers and souls, notes that kiddushin with money is learned from its purchase, and asks why a wedding should be learned from a grave. He answers that Avraham wanted his bond with Sarah to continue beyond life, since a Jewish marriage is a union of souls that existed before birth.

title.en: The bar mitzvah as a wedding with the Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah should be celebrated like a wedding, since the boy then receives his soul, which is Torah, and tells how Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai married off his son the night he turned thirteen. Through 'morasha kehillas Yaakov' and the Chasam Sofer on Haman he shows that the Torah is the inheritance and kallah of every Jew.

title.en: Efron's dust and the fire of zrizus

summary.en: The Rav ties the bar mitzvah to the parsha: Efron was a klipah in Chevron blocking the way to the Machpelah, and Avraham overcame it. Building on the father's words about the name Naftali Tzvi, he contrasts the fire of zrizus with the dust of Efron and sadness, then says the holy ancestors attend the simcha and blesses the boy.

catalogTitle: קליפת נוגה בארבע יסודות. חילוק בין תיקון חטא דקליפת נוגה וחטא דשלש קליפות הטמאות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 7, the Rav explains how the permitted pleasures of kelipas nogah can be raised back to kedushah, why forbidden things stay bound until the final redemption, and how teshuvah from love turns even sins into merits.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tanya chapter 7. After the example of a light word said to lift the mood for learning, he turns to one who eats meat and drinks wine for pleasure alone. Pleasure comes from the element of water; such eating draws the food down into kelipas nogah. Because kosher food is 'heter', untied, it rises again when its energy is used for avodas Hashem, while forbidden food is 'asur', tied to the three impure kelipos. He explains that a person's possessions are sparks of his own soul, placed with him by hashgacha pratis, and why later generations added chumros. Even raised, permitted indulgence leaves a mark that the beating of the grave removes, while forbidden food needs Gehinnom or the end of death itself. He discusses samples of that future purification, and closes with teshuvah from love, which raises the baal teshuvah above the tzaddik and turns sins into merits.

en: Pleasure derives from the element of water, and eating meat or drinking wine only for pleasure draws them down into kelipas nogah.
Kosher food eaten for pleasure can rise back to kedushah when its energy is later used for avodas Hashem, because 'heter' means untied; forbidden food is 'asur', tied to the impure kelipos.
Everything a person owns holds sparks of his own soul, brought to him by hashgacha pratis, and using it for Heaven's sake redeems them.

Even after permitted indulgence is raised, a mark remains in the body; it is cleansed by the beating of the grave, while what is absorbed from forbidden food needs Gehinnom or the end of death in the future.
Teshuvah from great love reaches the level of the future redemption and can release even forbidden things; a baal teshuvah's sins become merits because they fueled his return.

title.en: Review, and a light word for a good purpose

summary.en: The Rav reviews that deeds in thought, speech and action can tilt to kedushah or to the impure kelipos, then explains the Tanya's example of saying something humorous to lighten the mood so that one can learn and daven better.

title.en: The four elements and the pleasure of water

summary.en: The Rav turns to those who eat meat and drink wine only to satisfy desire. He explains the four elements, that every pleasure comes from the element of water, and why wine is especially dangerous, bringing a remark on the words of Kiddush.

title.en: Heter is untied, issur is bound

summary.en: The Rav explains that kosher meat and wine eaten for desire fall into kelipas nogah but rise back when he uses their energy for avodas Hashem, because a permitted thing is 'untied'; forbidden food stays bound and its energy cannot raise Torah.

title.en: Sparks of the soul in one's possessions

summary.en: The Rav explains that by exact hashgacha pratis every possession, his yarmulke, his bread, his home, carries sparks related to his soul, which he redeems by using them for Heaven's sake. He illustrates with a lost yarmulke, a broken glass and a loaf of bread, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Rambam on health.

title.en: Why later generations added chumros

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Rema forbids things the Gemara permits. He explains that borderline items could once be refined by great souls through their avodah and brachos, but later poskim saw that such things are now bound by thin strings that this generation cannot cut.

title.en: The mark that remains in the body

summary.en: Reading the Tanya that a mark of the indulgence remains in the body, the Rav compares it to a stain left on a shirt, connects it to Rashi on a tzaddik leaving a mark, explains why fervent young people can grow coarse with age, and brings that the beating of the grave removes this mark.

title.en: Dust and stains: the grave, Gehinnom and the end of death

summary.en: With the mashal of a dusty mattress beaten clean versus a cloth that needs hot water, the Rav explains that permitted indulgence is removed by the beating of the grave and forbidden pleasure by Gehinnom, while what is fully bound rises only when death is swallowed up forever.

title.en: Samples of the future purification

summary.en: The Rav brings the question how Moshe Rabbeinu could use Egyptian animals that had been worshipped as korbanos, and the Satmar Rav's answer that Yetzias Mitzrayim was a local sample of the future end of tumah. He adds the Rema on adorning the Seder table with pledged vessels and explains bitul b'shishim as a case Hashem arranges, which a person may not do himself.

title.en: Teshuvah from love: a private redemption

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya that teshuvah from great love, with a thirst like parched land, releases even forbidden things, a private sample of the future redemption. He brings that baalei teshuvah stand where complete tzaddikim cannot, and the Zohar's mashal of a bird escaping from a hand.

title.en: Sins become merits

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sin itself caused the baal teshuvah's higher level, so it is rectified at its root and becomes a merit, as Chazal say. He ends with a question on Rashi about a tzaddik son of a rasha and a tzaddik son of a tzaddik.
